story.title: Juno and the Bee Who Met Dinosaurs
story.subtitle: A tiny buzzing guide takes Juno on a sweet honey adventure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Amber Bead
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor with her dinosaurs. She lined up Stego, Rex, and Trike in a row.

Under the toy box, something sparkled. It was a little golden bead, shiny and hard.

Juno picked it up. It began to glow. It began to hum, soft and low.

POP! A tiny bee buzzed out and landed on Juno's thumb.

"Hello!" said the bee. "I'm Buzz. This bead is amber — old tree goo that turned hard as stone. A bee got stuck inside it, long, long ago. Back when dinosaurs walked around!"

Juno's eyes went wide. "A bee met a dinosaur?"

"Yep! Want to see my hive? Hold my wing and shrink down with me."

Juno grabbed on. WHOOOOSH! The bedroom got very big.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Busy Buzzing Home
chapters.text:
They landed by a round, papery ball. It buzzed like a hundred tiny engines.

"This is the hive," said Buzz. "Our bee home."

Inside, bees zoomed everywhere. One big bee sat calm in the middle.

"That's our queen," said Buzz. "She lays the eggs. Up to 2,000 a day, in busy springtime!"

Juno counted on her fingers and gave up fast. "That's SO many!"

"All the other girl bees are workers," said Buzz. "They do every job — cleaning, guarding the door, finding flowers. A hive can hold up to 80,000 bees in summer!"

Juno peeked at a sleepy bee in the corner. "Who's that?"

"A drone. A boy bee. There's only a few."

Juno giggled. "Bee families are BIG!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
A worker bee landed and wiggled, round and round, in little figure-eights.

Juno copied the wiggle. "Is she dancing?"

"She is! It's called a waggle dance. It tells the other bees which way to fly, and how far, to find yummy flowers."

Juno wiggled again, pointing one arm toward the window. "Like this?"

"Exactly like that! A scientist named Karl figured out what the dance meant. He watched bees for years and years."

Juno pointed her arm at a pretend flower on the carpet. "Follow me, bees!"

A whole cloud of bees lifted off and followed her wiggling arm, right out the door.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Sip, Sip, Sip
chapters.text:
Outside, flowers stretched as far as Juno could see.

Each bee landed, dipped down, and sipped sweet flower juice. Buzz called it nectar.

"One bee only makes a tiny, tiny bit of honey, her whole life long," said Buzz. "Smaller than one drop!"

Juno looked at the huge field. "How many flowers do you need, then?"

"All the bees together visit about two million flowers," said Buzz, "just to make one pound of honey."

Juno's mouth dropped open. "TWO MILLION?!"

"That's why we all work together," said Buzz, sipping from a daisy. "Teamwork makes honey work."

Juno picked the next flower. A sunny yellow one. The bees zoomed toward it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Six Little Sides
chapters.text:
Back in the hive, bees built little shelves out of wax.

Juno leaned close. "They're all the same shape!"

"Good eye," said Buzz. "Count the sides for me."

Juno counted slowly with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"Six sides make a hexagon," said Buzz. "Bees build this honeycomb with hexagons because it holds the most honey, using the least wax. Clever, right?"

Juno pressed her finger gently into an empty wax cup. It fit just right.

"Can I fill one?" Juno asked.

Buzz handed her a drop of nectar. Juno poured it in. PLOP. One tiny cup, done.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Five Eyes and Fast Wings
chapters.text:
A bee zoomed close to Juno's face. BZZZZZZ.

"Why's it so loud?" Juno asked, covering her ears and giggling.

"Her wings flap 200 times every single second," said Buzz. "That's what makes the buzz."

Juno looked closer at the bee's face. "Whoa, how many eyes does she have?"

"Five! Two big ones for seeing shapes and colors, and three tiny ones on top, just for sensing light."

Juno tried to count them, nose almost touching the bee. The bee didn't mind one bit.

"Five eyes AND fast wings," said Juno. "Bees are basically superheroes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Honey That Never Goes Bad
chapters.text:
Buzz led Juno to a jar of deep gold honey.

"Honey almost never goes bad," said Buzz. "Long, long ago, in Egypt, people drew pictures of beekeepers on walls. That was thousands and thousands of years ago."

"Did their honey go yucky?" Juno asked, wrinkling her nose.

"Nope! People even found old honey, sealed up tight, and it was still good to eat!"

Juno dipped her finger in and tasted a tiny bit. "Mmm! Still yummy."

"Still yummy," Buzz agreed, "after all that time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again, Bellies Full
chapters.text:
"One more thing," said Buzz. "Bees help grow lots of food. Apples, blueberries, almonds — about one of every three yummy bites you eat!"

Juno gasped. "Even my apple snack?"

"Even your apple snack."

Buzz flew Juno gently back toward her bedroom. WHOOOOSH, she grew big again, right on the carpet, next to her dinosaurs.

The amber bead sat quiet now, just a little gold bead again. But next to it was something new: one tiny golden drop of honey, shiny on the carpet.

Juno smiled and tucked the bead under her pillow.

"Goodnight, Buzz," she whispered. "Goodnight, bees."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Sweet dreams, little wonderer.

fact_pack.summary: Bees are flying insects living almost everywhere flowers grow, and a honeybee hive works together like one giant family. Beyond making honey, bees pollinate much of the food people eat, and scientists still study how these tiny insects talk and find their way home.

facts.text: A honeybee colony usually has one queen, tens of thousands of female worker bees, and a smaller number of male drones.
A healthy queen bee can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day during the busy spring season.
Worker bees are all female and take turns doing every job in the hive, from cleaning cells to guarding the entrance to flying out to find flowers.
A drone's only job is to mate with a queen, and hives push drones out before winter because they cannot forage or sting to help defend the colony.
Scientists have described roughly 20,000 species of bees around the world, and only a few of them, like the honeybee, make the honey people eat.
Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch discovered that honeybees perform a 'waggle dance' to tell each other a flower's direction and distance.
Karl von Frisch won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973 for figuring out how bees communicate through dance and scent.
One worker honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire lifetime.
Bees in a colony together may visit roughly two million flowers to gather enough nectar to make just one pound of honey.
Because honey has very little water and is naturally acidic, sealed pots of honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs are still edible thousands of years later.
A bee has five eyes in total: two large compound eyes for seeing shapes and colors, plus three tiny simple eyes on top of its head for sensing light.
A honeybee's wings beat about 200 times every second, and that fast flapping is what makes the buzzing sound people hear.
Only female bees have a stinger, and a honeybee worker's stinger is barbed so it stays in mammal skin, which means she dies soon after she stings.
Bees and other pollinators help produce roughly one out of every three bites of food humans eat, including apples, blueberries, and almonds.
Each spring, truckloads of honeybee hives are shipped into California to pollinate its almond orchards.
Beekeepers began widely reporting Colony Collapse Disorder in 2006, when many adult worker bees mysteriously left their hives and did not return.
Researchers link colony losses to several causes together: mites, disease, pesticides, and lost flowering habitat.
Honeycomb cells are built in a six-sided hexagon shape because it lets bees store the most honey while using the least amount of wax.
On cold days bees cluster and shiver their flight muscles to keep the hive near 95°F (35°C).
Bees preserved in amber roughly 100 million years old show bees lived alongside dinosaurs.
Egyptian wall art from around 2400 BC shows beekeepers collecting honeycomb, among the oldest farming records.
A single honeybee hive can hold 20,000 to 80,000 bees at the height of summer.

Egyptian art shows people keeping bees and collecting honey
Karl von Frisch wins the Nobel Prize for decoding the bee waggle dance
Colony Collapse Disorder is first widely reported in the United States

story.title: Omar and the Bell That Remembered Every Bike
story.subtitle: A BMX kid rides two hundred years of wheels, one DING at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell in the Garage
chapters.text:
Omar balanced on his back wheel, pedaling slow, nose up, eyes forward. Wheelies were his favorite trick, and tonight he had held one for ten whole seconds. He rolled into the garage to park his bike for the night.

On a dusty shelf sat an old bike bell, bent and rusty. Omar had never seen it before. He gave it a flick. DING!

The bell flashed bright green. A tiny glowing rider popped out of the sound, spinning like a BMX trick done in slow motion.

"Name's Dinger," said the rider, landing on Omar's handlebars. "Want to see where your bike came from? Ring me three times."

Omar loved a good dare. DING. DING. DING! The garage spun into green mist. WHOOOSH!

They landed on a dusty street in Germany, in the year **1817**. A man in a tall hat wobbled past on a strange wooden two-wheeler with handlebars — but **no pedals at all**.

"That's **Karl von Drais**," said Dinger. "He built this and called it a running machine."

Omar watched the man push along with his feet, like pushing a skateboard. "He's basically scooting," Omar said.

"People nicknamed it the **hobby horse**," said Dinger, "and it steers with handlebars, same as yours."

Omar hopped on a spare one, pushed off with both feet, then lifted his feet like a glide trick at the skate park.

"I could land this at the park!" Omar laughed.

DING! The bell glowed again, ready for the next stop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker Bumps
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They landed on a bumpy cobblestone road in France, in the **1860s**. A man rolled by on a bike with pedals bolted straight onto the front wheel.

"**Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement** added those pedals," said Dinger. "People called this ride the velocipede. But everyone used a nickname — the **boneshaker**."

Omar felt every bump through his sneakers. "Why boneshaker?"

"Ride it over these stones and you'll shake like jelly," said Dinger.

Omar tried a lap, teeth rattling, just like rolling his BMX over a cracked sidewalk too fast. "This is rougher than the skate park ramps!" he laughed.

"Lallement even got a patent for this pedal design in America, in **1866**," Dinger added.

Omar hopped off, rubbing his elbow. "Next stop, something smoother, please!"

DING!

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header
chapters.text:
They landed beside a giant wheel. Omar tilted his head back to see the top of it. A rider perched way up high, pedaling a wheel almost as tall as a door.

"This is a **penny-farthing**," said Dinger. "Named for two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing — because of the two different-sized wheels."

"One pedal turn and you go further," Dinger said, "because the front wheel is so huge."

Omar watched the rider wobble. "That looks like it could really go wrong."

"It could," said Dinger. "Riders sat so high, a sudden stop could toss them right over the handlebars. People called that **taking a header**."

The rider hit a rock, tipped, and tumbled into a soft hay cart waiting nearby. He popped up laughing, hay in his hair.

Omar laughed too. "Good thing bikes got better after this one."

DING!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle
chapters.text:
They landed in England, **1885**. A man named **John Kemp Starley** wheeled out a brand-new bike. Omar's eyes went wide — it looked almost normal!

"Two wheels, same size," Omar said. "And look — a chain!"

"That's the **Rover Safety Bicycle**," said Dinger. "The chain spins the back wheel, so nobody needs a giant front wheel anymore."

Omar crouched to look at the chain looping around two metal gears, just like the one on his own BMX. "This is way closer to mine," he said.

"Much safer too," said Dinger. "No more headers. This design became the one the whole world copied."

Omar hopped on, pedaled a slow circle, and popped a tiny bunny hop off a curb, just because he could.

"Okay," Omar said, "THIS one I'd ride to the skate park."

DING!
chapters.shout_line: THIS one I'd ride to the skate park!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Bouncy Tires
chapters.text:
They landed in a backyard in Scotland, **1888**. A man named **John Boyd Dunlop** knelt by a tricycle, wrapping its wheel in a rubber tube full of air.

"My son's ride was too bumpy," Dunlop said. "So I made the wheels bouncy instead."

Omar pressed the tire with his thumb. It squished and sprang back, just like his own BMX tires. "Air inside! That's why mine feel bouncy at the park."

"Exactly," said Dinger. "Before this, tires were solid rubber, hard as a rock. Dunlop's air-filled tire made every ride smoother."

"His company turned into **Dunlop Tyres**," Dinger added. "Still around today, on bikes and cars."

Omar gave the tire a thump of approval. "Good thinking, Dunlop."

DING!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age
chapters.text:
They landed in a busy street packed with bicycles, in the **1890s**. Omar had never seen so many bikes in one place.

"This is the **Golden Age of Bicycles**," said Dinger. "Millions got sold across Europe and America."

A woman zoomed past wearing baggy pants instead of a long skirt. "Those look comfy," Omar said.

"Long skirts could get caught in the wheels," said Dinger, "so people started wearing roomier pants called **bloomers** instead."

"A woman named **Susan B. Anthony** said bikes gave women more freedom than almost anything else," Dinger said. "Suddenly, people could go wherever they pedaled."

Omar nodded. "Bikes just kept making life better."

A hundred bells jingled from every direction, like a chorus of DINGs.

DING!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Flew
chapters.text:
They landed outside a small shop in **Dayton, Ohio**, in the 1890s. A sign read Wright Cycle Company.

Two brothers, **Wilbur and Orville Wright**, were fixing a bicycle wheel, spokes gleaming in the sun.

"They fixed and built bikes here," said Dinger, "before they became famous for something else."

Omar peered at the thin metal tubing. "This looks light, like race bike parts."

"Good eye," said Dinger. "They used that same lightweight tubing and those spoked wheels later — to build the first successful airplane, in **1903**."

Omar's jaw dropped. "Bike guys invented FLYING?"

"Pedal power to wing power," said Dinger, grinning.

Omar pictured a bike with wings and nearly fell over laughing.

DING!

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Garage
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They landed somewhere dusty and dirt-packed, in the **1970s**. Riders did jumps on small, sturdy bikes.

"**BMX bikes**," said Dinger. "Built tough for tricks and dirt racing, like the motorcycles they got the idea from. **Mountain bikes** came along too, with wide bumpy tires for rough trails."

Omar beamed. "Finally, MY kind of bike!"

"Today there are more than **a billion bicycles** on Earth," said Dinger. "More than any other ride, anywhere."

DING! The green mist swirled, and the garage reappeared around them.

Omar stood holding the old bell, now gleaming instead of rusty. Dinger waved from inside the DING, smaller and smaller.

"Thanks for the ride through every ride," Omar said, setting the bell gently on his handlebars.

He rolled his bike inside, the bell shining soft green in the dark, like it was still humming with two hundred years of wheels.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ring well, and roll on.

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Sam and Spark Climb the Walls
story.subtitle: A tiny-sized tour of sticky feet, squishy hooves, and gooey toes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Spider in the Grass
chapters.text:
Sam knelt in the cool evening grass. A little spider walked across his hand. Its legs tickled like tiny feathers.

"Hello, friend," Sam said. He loved spiders. He loved geckos too. He picked up every bug he could find in the yard.

Something glowed green by the fence. A tiny toy gecko blinked its eyes. Its tail flashed brighter and brighter.

"Finally," said the gecko. "I've been waiting for a kid who likes bugs as much as I do."

Sam's jaw dropped. Toys don't talk!

"I'm Spark," said the gecko. "Want to see how animals climb walls?"

"YES!" Sam shouted, so loud a bird flew off the fence.

Spark's tail flashed bright green. WHOOOSH! The whole yard spun around. Sam felt small. Smaller. Tiny!

He looked up. Blades of grass towered over him like trees.

"Whoa," Sam whispered. "I'm tiny!"

"Tiny enough to see the secrets," Spark said. "Follow me, bug buddy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gecko on the Window
chapters.text:
Spark led tiny Sam to a sunny window. A real gecko ran straight up the glass. Then it walked upside down, right across the ceiling, like the ceiling was the floor.

"How does he do that?" Sam asked. "He's not glued on!"

"Look closer," Spark said.

Sam pressed close to the gecko's foot. He saw rows and rows of tiny hairs. So many they looked fuzzy, like fur.

"Millions of tiny hairs," Spark said. "Scientists call them setae, which just means tiny sticky hairs. Each one is thinner than your eyelash."

Sam tried to count them. "One, two, three..." He gave up at twenty. "There's SO many!"

"Each little hair holds on with a teeny, tiny tug," Spark said. "Not sticky like glue. More like a secret handshake with the glass."

Sam tried to run up the window himself. His sneaker squeaked. He slid right back down. THUMP!

Spark giggled so hard his tail blinked twice. "No hairs on your feet, buddy."

Sam laughed too, rubbing his bottom. "Worth a try!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
"Does he ever get stuck forever?" Sam asked. "Like gum stuck in hair?"

"Nope," said Spark. "It's not glue at all. No mess, ever."

The gecko peeled one toe up. Then the next. Then the next. Just like pulling up a sticker, one corner at a time.

Sam had a sticker on his hand from show-and-tell. He peeled it the exact same way. "Just like that!"

"Exactly like that," Spark said. "Peel, peel, peel, toe by toe."

"His feet stay clean too," Spark added. "Dust just rolls right off every time he takes a step."

Sam looked down at his own dusty sneakers. "I wish MY feet did that."

Spark laughed. "Maybe skip the mud puddles next time."

The gecko zoomed across the ceiling and vanished behind a lamp.

"Bye, gecko friend!" Sam called, waving both hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Fly on the Ceiling
chapters.text:
A fly buzzed by and landed on the ceiling. It did not fall.

Sam squinted up at it. "Does he have hairs too?"

Spark shook his tiny head. "Look at his feet. Really, really close."

Sam looked. He saw tiny shiny drops, like dew sitting on grass.

"It's sticky goo!" Sam shouted. "His feet make little glue drops!"

"You got it," Spark said. "Flies, and some beetles too, ooze sticky liquid from tiny pads. Like walking around on wet glue stamps."

The fly buzzed off, leaving tiny shiny dots behind on the ceiling.

Sam reached out one finger. A tiny drop stuck to his fingertip. He pulled his finger away. The goo stretched like gum, then snapped back.

"Sticky!" Sam giggled, shaking his sticky hand.

Spark laughed so hard his whole tail blinked. "Gross and cool," he said. "The best combo there is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sam's Favorite Spider
chapters.text:
Back near the window, Sam spotted his garden spider again. It walked straight up the glass, easy as pie.

Sam gasped. "Wait. Spiders climb glass too! Are their feet like gecko feet?"

Spark beamed. "Smart catch, Sam. Spiders have thousands of teeny hairs too. Scientists call them setules. Same idea as gecko hairs, just spider-sized."

Sam puffed up with pride. "I KNEW spiders were cool."

"You always know," Spark said. "That's why I picked you, bug buddy."

The spider spun a tiny thread and lowered itself gently onto Sam's open palm. Its legs tickled like before.

Sam watched it for a moment, smiling. Then he set it back on a leaf. "Off you go, buddy. Climb safe."

"I bet nobody at school knows spider hairs are secretly like gecko hairs," Sam said.

"Now you do," said Spark. "Lucky them, having you around."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Ants on the Brick Wall
chapters.text:
Spark zoomed tiny Sam to a brick wall. A long line of ants marched straight up it.

"Rough bricks are easy for them," Spark said. "Ants use tiny claws, like little climbing hooks."

The ants reached a smooth glass door. They slowed down but kept right on going.

Sam watched closely. "They're walking different now! Slower, and kind of flat-footed."

"Good eyes," Spark said. "On smooth stuff, they switch to sticky pads on their feet instead of claws. Like swapping climbing boots for sticky socks."

"Ants have TWO climbing tools?" Sam said. "Lucky ants!"

"Cockroaches do the very same trick," Spark added.

Sam shivered just a tiny bit, then grinned anyway. "Still cool. Even roaches."

"Can I have sticky socks too?" Sam asked.

"Maybe for your birthday," Spark said, winking his glowing eye.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain Goat's Trick
chapters.text:
Spark's tail flashed again. The ants vanished. Now Sam stood near a tall, rocky cliff.

A mountain goat stood on a ledge thinner than a shelf.

"How does he not fall?" Sam asked, eyes wide.

"Look at his hooves," Spark said. A hoof is like a hard, curved shoe an animal is born with.

Sam peeked close. The hoof had a hard edge, like a fingernail. "What's inside, though? It looks squishy in the middle."

"Good guess!" Spark said. "The middle really is soft and squishy. It squishes into every little bump on the rock."

"Like a shoe that hugs the rock!" Sam said, clapping.

The goat hopped to another ledge. A few tiny rocks tumbled down below and landed softly, far away. Nobody was in any danger at all. The goat was simply great at his job.

"He's basically a rock-climbing champion," Sam said.

"Best in the whole mountain," Spark agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Squirrel and the Way Back Home
chapters.text:
Spark's tail flashed one more time. Sam landed back in his own backyard, Sam-sized again, not tiny anymore.

A squirrel scurried up the oak tree beside him, fast as a wink.

"How does he climb so quick?" Sam asked.

"Sharp, curved claws," Spark said. "They dig into teeny cracks and bumps you can't even see."

Sam touched the tree bark. It looked smooth, but felt rough under his fingers. "Tiny hiding spots!"

"Exactly," Spark said. "Every climber has a trick. Hairs, goo, claws, squishy hooves, sticky socks."

Sam grinned a huge grin. "And I found them ALL tonight."

Spark's tail glowed warm now, soft like a nightlight.

Sam picked up a tiny pebble from the grass, his keepsake from the whole tiny adventure, and tucked it deep in his pajama pocket.

He yawned a giant yawn.

"Time for bed," Spark said softly. "Stick with it, little climber."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Stick with it, little climber.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

story.title: Milo and Juno and the Brick That Clicks
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the whole history of LEGO.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping together a LEGO shark. Its fin was gray and spiky.

Juno sat close by, roaring her plastic dinosaur. "Rawr! My dinosaur is bigger than your shark!"

"No way," laughed Milo. "My shark has a hundred teeth!"

Then one little brick on the carpet began to glow gold. It hummed, soft and low.

Milo picked it up. It felt warm, like sunshine on a pillow.

CLICK! The brick popped open like a tiny door. A tiny voice said, "Want to see where I came from?"

"Who are you?" asked Juno.

"I'm Brix," said the voice. "I'm the very first brick ever made."

WHOOOOSH! The floor swirled into gold light. Milo and Juno tumbled right through the little door.

They landed in a wooden workshop that smelled like fresh sawdust. A man with kind eyes was carving a toy duck.

"Who are you?" Milo asked.

"I'm Ole Kirk," the man said. "I'm a **carpenter** — that means I build things out of wood. I started this workshop in **Billund, Denmark**, back in **1932**."

Milo looked at the shelves. Wooden ducks, trucks, and little stepladders were everywhere.

"Do you ever give up?" Juno asked.

Ole Kirk smiled. "Never. I just try again, and again, and again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well!
chapters.text:
A painter stood on a ladder outside, brush in hand. He was painting big letters over the workshop door.

"L... E..." Milo read slowly. "What does it spell?"

The painter grinned down at him. "Go on, guess!"

Juno bounced on her toes. "G! O!"

"**LEGO**!" Milo shouted.

Ole Kirk stepped outside, wiping his hands on his apron. "That's right! In **1934**, I named my company LEGO. It comes from two Danish words — ***leg godt*** — which mean **'play well.'**"

"Play well," Juno repeated, trying the new words out slowly.

Brix the little brick hummed happily. "Some people also say *lego* means 'I put together,' in an old language called Latin. That's a fun story — but it was probably just a happy accident, not the real reason for the name."

Milo giggled. "Either way, it fits perfectly."

"PLAY WELL!" the children shouted together, and somewhere down the street, a dog barked right back at them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Machine
chapters.text:
Years rolled by in a blink, like pages flipping fast in a book.

Brix led them into a loud room full of clanking machines. "This is **1947**," he said. "Ole Kirk just got a brand new machine."

The machine hissed and squirted warm, melted plastic into little metal molds.

"Whoa!" said Milo. "It's like a squeezy glue gun, but GIANT!"

"Exactly," said Brix. "It was one of the very first plastic-squirting machines in all of Denmark."

Juno pointed at a tray of shiny new toys, still warm from the machine. "They're shiny!"

"Plastic doesn't break as easily as wood," said Brix, "and it never gets soggy in the bathtub."

Milo grinned. "Good. My shark bath toys need to survive Juno's tidal waves."

Juno splashed her hands through the air. "SPLOOSH!"

She splashed again, just to hear Milo laugh.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Hollow Bricks
chapters.text:
The room shifted around them. Now shelves held little studded bricks, bright red and sunshine yellow.

"**1949**," said Brix. "These are called Automatic Binding Bricks. They're hollow underneath, like a little cup turned upside down."

Milo picked one up and peeked at the bottom. "It's empty under there!"

"Exactly," said Brix. "That empty space lets it sit right on top of another brick's bumps."

Juno tried stacking two bricks together. She pressed hard.

They wiggled loose and tumbled apart with a tiny clatter.

"They don't hold very well yet," Juno said, a tiny frown on her face.

"You're right," said Brix gently. "That's the next problem to solve."

Milo tapped his chin, the way he did when building something tricky at home.

"Maybe they need something extra inside," he said slowly.

Brix's light flickered with excitement. "Hang on to that thought, Milo."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Brick With Tubes
chapters.text:
A young man sat at a table, turning a brick over and over in his hands. This was Godtfred, Ole Kirk's own son.

"Milo," Brix whispered, "tell him your idea."

Milo cleared his throat. "What if there were little rings inside, so they could grab onto the bumps below, like fingers holding tight?"

Godtfred's eyebrows shot up. "Rings... inside..." He grabbed a pencil and sketched tiny round shapes into the brick's hollow bottom.

Juno lined up two of the new bricks and pressed them together.

**CLICK!**

She pulled. It held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" the children yelled.

"This new brick became official on **January 28, 1958**," said Brix. "And here's the amazing part. A brick made that very day still clicks perfectly with a brick made today."

Milo looked back toward home, thinking of his own LEGO shark. "So my shark brick could click with THIS one?"

"That exact one," said Brix, glowing proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Park Next Door
chapters.text:
Brix whisked them forward again. Blinking in bright sunlight, they stood outside the very same factory — but now there was a whole park right next door!

Juno spotted it first. "Look! There's a tiny town made of bricks over there!"

"Sharp eyes," said Brix. "That's **LEGOLAND**, in **Billund**. It opened right beside the factory in **1968**."

Milo ran toward a model town built entirely from LEGO bricks — tiny houses, tiny cars, even a tiny harbor with little brick ships bobbing along.

"It's like our bedroom floor," Milo laughed, "but giant, and outside, and nobody steps on it by accident."

Juno giggled. "I step on bricks ALL the time. Ouch, ouch, ouch."

Brix's light twinkled. "Lucky for you, nobody steps on LEGOLAND."

They wandered the tiny streets until the sun began to dip low and gold.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bricks for Little Hands
chapters.text:
Brix led them past a shelf of extra-big, chunky bricks, perfect for small fingers.

"These are **DUPLO** bricks," said Brix. "They came out in **1969**. They're bigger, so even little hands like Juno's can build with them easily."

Juno picked one up. It was twice the size of Milo's bricks, easy to grip and squeeze.

"They still click together with the regular bricks too," Brix added. "Everything LEGO has ever made still fits together."

Juno stacked three DUPLO bricks into a wobbly dinosaur shape, humming to herself as she worked.

"My dino!" she announced proudly.

Milo clicked a tiny LEGO shark fin onto the DUPLO dinosaur's back.

"Now it's a dino-shark!" he said.

Juno dissolved into giggles. "Best. Toy. Ever."

She hugged the wobbly dino-shark tight against her chest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"Time to go home," said Brix gently. The gold light swirled again, soft as a lullaby.

WHOOOOSH! Milo and Juno landed back on their own bedroom carpet, right where they had started.

Milo looked down at his hand. The little golden brick was still there, warm and glowing faintly.

He clicked it onto the bottom of his LEGO shark. It fit perfectly, just like Brix had promised a brick always would.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn and hugged her wobbly dino-shark close.

"Goodnight, Brix," Milo whispered.

The little brick gave one last happy hum, then rested quietly on the carpet beside the shark — a tiny keepsake from a very big adventure.

Outside, the whole street had gone quiet and dark, and the only light left in the room was one small, sleepy gold glow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

facts.text: Carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen founded the company in Billund, Denmark, in 1932, first making wooden toys and stepladders.
In 1934 Christiansen named his company LEGO, a shortening of the Danish phrase 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well.'
A popular story notes that 'lego' also happens to mean 'I put together' in Latin, though this seems to be a happy coincidence rather than the real reason for the name.
LEGO began working with plastic in 1947, becoming one of the first Danish companies to own a plastic injection-molding machine.
In 1949 the company produced 'Automatic Binding Bricks,' hollow studded plastic bricks that were the direct ancestor of the modern LEGO brick.
Ole Kirk's son Godtfred Kirk Christiansen redesigned the brick with hollow tubes underneath, and the new locking brick was patented on 28 January 1958.
A brick made in 1958 still fits perfectly with a LEGO brick made today because the tube-and-stud design has barely changed.
A 1960 fire destroyed the company's wooden-toy warehouse, and afterward the family decided to stop making wooden toys and focus only on plastic bricks.
In 1963 LEGO switched its brick material to ABS plastic, which resists cracking and keeps its color much better than the earlier plastic.
The first LEGOLAND theme park opened in Billund in 1968, right next to the original factory.
DUPLO bricks, sized just right for toddlers and still compatible with regular LEGO bricks, were introduced in 1969.
The LEGO Technic line, adding gears, axles and beams for more mechanical builds, launched in 1977.
The first LEGO minifigures, with movable arms and swappable heads and hats, appeared in 1978.
Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, grandson of the founder, took over leadership of the company in 1979, keeping it in family hands for another generation.
Because so many tiny rubber tires are made for LEGO sets, the company is sometimes called one of the world's biggest tire producers by count, though it makes no full-size tires.
LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets in 1999, beginning a long line of licensed themes based on movies and games.
The Fortune Encyclopedia and other outlets named the LEGO brick a top 'Toy of the Century' around the year 2000.
In the early 2000s the LEGO Group ran into serious financial trouble and came close to bankruptcy.
Jorgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO in 2004 and led a turnaround that focused the company back on its core brick sets.
In 2014 The LEGO Movie brought LEGO characters to cinemas worldwide and became a major box-office success.
The LEGO Group is still headquartered in Billund, Denmark, on the same ground where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood.
The Kirkbi family, descendants of Ole Kirk Christiansen, remain the majority owners of the LEGO Group today.

story.title: Isla and the Lamp of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A true mystery buried in ash for almost seventeen hundred years

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Dig in the Shoebox
chapters.text:
Isla had turned her bedroom floor into a dig site. Six shoeboxes, each labeled in marker — SITE ONE, SITE TWO — held her finds: a snail shell (#14), a chip of blue sea glass (#9), a bent house key nobody could identify (#22, still a mystery). She liked the mystery part best. Anyone could pick up an object. Figuring out its story was the actual job.

The box from Grandma's attic was new. It smelled like dust and old pennies, and at the bottom, under a photograph and a broken watch, sat a small clay lamp — the oil-burning kind, with a chipped spout and a pattern worn almost smooth.

Isla held her magnifying glass over it and squinted. Under the grime, scratched into the clay, were letters. She rubbed with her thumb until she could read them.

"P-O-M... Pompeii," she said out loud, testing the word. "I know that name. That's the one buried by the volcano."

The lamp went warm in her hand. A thread of grey smoke curled up from the spout — it smelled of salt and ash, like a campfire by the sea — and the smoke didn't drift away. It hung in the air and folded itself into a shape: a hillside, a blue bay, tiny figures with shovels.

"That's not how smoke works," Isla said, which was a very reasonable thing to say, and then she leaned in anyway, because some mysteries you solve with your brain and some you solve by walking straight into them.

The smoke wrapped around her like a sleeve. It didn't feel cold or frightening — more like stepping into a held breath. A voice that seemed to come from the lamp itself, warm and a little amused, said: "I only show what's true. You can touch, you can look, you can ask — but nothing in there can touch you back." Then the warm light swallowed the bedroom whole.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Diggers in the Dark
chapters.text:
Isla landed on her feet in a trench, sunlight slanting low, the smell of turned earth everywhere. Men in old-fashioned clothes were digging with picks, piling grey, crumbly rock to one side. It was the year 1748 — the lamp's smoke had whispered the date into her ear like a caption.

"Nobody had found this place in ages," Isla murmured. "They're not digging up something new. They're digging up something **forgotten**."

One of the workers knelt, brushed dirt from something pale, and lifted out a chunk of painted plaster. He turned it over, frowning, clearly as puzzled as she was.

"What is this place even called?" Isla asked the smoke.

"Pompeii," it answered. "Some people think the name comes from an old word, *pompe*, from a language called Oscan that isn't spoken anymore. It might mean 'five' — maybe because five little villages joined together to build one town, a long time before any of this digging. Nobody's completely sure, but it's the best guess anyone has."

Isla crouched and pushed her hand into the trench wall, feeling the layers — ash, then rock, then ash again, taller than she was. She held her arm up against it to measure.

"This is deep," she said. "Like — over my head, twice."

"Good eye," said the smoke. "In places it's **four to six meters** — thirteen to twenty feet — of ash and volcanic rock on top of this town. That's why nobody found it for so long. It wasn't lost. It was buried."

A worker's pick struck something that didn't shatter like rock. Isla pointed before anyone else noticed. "There — that sound was different."

The man dug around it carefully and lifted out a curved roof tile, whole, its edge still sharp. He held it up to the light, grinning, and the other diggers crowded round.

"That tile," the smoke said, "is one of the first proper finds that told people: there's a whole town down here." Isla grinned back at nobody in particular. She'd spotted it first.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Town Wakes Up
chapters.text:
The smoke folded time again, and the trench vanished. Isla stood on a paved street in bright sun, and the town around her wasn't broken anymore — it was alive. Shop shutters banged open. Someone was selling bread. A bathhouse down the street let out a puff of steam.

"This is before," Isla said, understanding all at once. "This is Pompeii still standing."

"Around **11,000 to 15,000 people** lived here," said the smoke. "Shops, bathhouses, theaters, temples. A whole busy town near the sea, close to where the city of Naples is today."

A boy about sixteen fell into step beside her, ink-stained fingers, a wax tablet tucked under one arm. He introduced himself as Pliny — "the younger one," he added, as if that explained everything, which, Isla would soon learn, it kind of did.

She noticed the street had raised stones laid across it like stepping-stones, with gaps between them. "Those are weird," she said, crouching to look. "Too high to just be decoration. And the gaps are exactly the width of—" she looked up at a passing cart's wheels. "The wheels. Carts roll through the gaps, and people cross on top without getting their feet wet."

"Correct," said Pliny, looking faintly impressed. "The street floods when it rains. Or when the fountains overflow." He nodded toward a stone fountain gushing water from a carved spout. "Pipes under the whole town. Lead ones. They carry water to fountains everywhere — nobody has to walk far to fill a jug."

On a wall near the amphitheater, someone had painted big block letters in red. "Is that... an advertisement?" Isla asked.

"A political one," Pliny said. "People paint the names of the men they want elected, right on the walls. Also adverts for the gladiator games." He pointed at the round stone building looming behind him. "Built about **70 BC**. One of the oldest arenas like it that anyone's ever found."

Isla laughed. "So Pompeii invented campaign posters."

"We invented the wall," Pliny said dryly. "The posters were just good use of space."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Letters Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The sky had gone strange — a color Isla didn't have a name for, somewhere between bruise and storm. The ground gave a low shudder under her sandals, except she wasn't wearing sandals, she was wearing her sneakers, and the smoke's voice reminded her gently: nothing here can touch you.

"What's the date?" she asked, because that felt like the important thing to pin down.

"**August 24th, 79 AD**," the smoke said.

Pliny had gone very still, watching the mountain behind the town — Vesuvius — pour a column of smoke and rock impossibly high into the sky.

"I'm going to write about this," he said quietly. "Two long letters. I'll describe exactly what the cloud looked like, how it spread out at the top like the branches of a tree."

"People believe you?" Isla asked.

"They believe me so much," Pliny said, with the particular dry pride of someone who knows he's about to become extremely famous for a school essay, "that for thousands of years afterward, scientists call this exact kind of enormous, violent eruption a **Plinian eruption**. After me."

"That's either the best or the worst thing to be famous for," Isla said.

"Can't argue with you there."

Across the bay, ships were turning toward the shore instead of away from it. "That's my uncle," Pliny said. "Pliny the Elder. He commands ships, and right now he's sailing straight at the mountain, not away from it, because people over there need rescuing."

Isla watched the little ships cut toward danger instead of from it, and something about that steadied her more than anything else that strange afternoon. "That's either very brave or very reckless," she said.

"With my uncle," Pliny said, "it's usually both."

The smoke thickened around the whole scene like a curtain closing. "This is where we step back," it said gently. "You've seen enough of this part. Let's see what it left behind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Frozen in a Flash
chapters.text:
The smoke cleared into silence — a town with no shoppers, no shouting, no steam from the bathhouse. Just stillness, and dust that had hardened into something like stone.

"It happened so fast," the smoke said, "that it froze the whole town exactly as it was, like someone pressed pause."

Isla stepped into a bakery. An oven sat cold in the corner, and inside it, pale and round and cracked across the top like a real loaf fresh from baking, sat a **loaf of bread**. It still had the baker's own mark pressed into the crust.

"That's—" Isla's voice dropped to a whisper without her meaning it to. "That's somebody's actual bread. From that actual morning."

"THE BREAD!" she said, louder, because some discoveries deserve volume.

"Diggers found it just like that," said the smoke. "Painted walls too — pictures called **frescoes**, paint right on wet plaster so it dries into the wall itself — still with their colors. Even writing people scratched into walls for fun, like ancient graffiti, still readable."

Isla traced a faded painting of a garden on the wall with one finger, careful not to touch. "And the people?" she asked, because she needed to ask it, and the smoke didn't dodge.

"Many people did get away," it said simply. "Others didn't. It's a sad true thing, and the town remembers it by remembering them carefully, not by dwelling on it. That's what all of this is, really — a very careful, very respectful kind of remembering."

Isla nodded, and let that sit for a moment, and then looked back at the small perfect loaf of bread, saved by accident, found on purpose, nearly two thousand years later.

"I'm glad someone found it," she said.

"So is everyone who's ever seen it since," said the smoke.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Other Town
chapters.text:
The smoke carried her down the coast, past a headland, into a second town — smaller, quieter, right on the water.

"Herculaneum," the smoke said. "The same eruption buried this town too. But not the same way."

Isla frowned at a wooden door, still hanging on its hinges, charred black but whole. "Wood doesn't usually last. It rots. How is there still an actual door?"

"Good question — that's the mystery right there," said the smoke. "Pompeii got buried in dry ash and chunks of light rock called **pumice** — stone so full of air bubbles it can float on water. Herculaneum got buried in something hotter and wetter, a thick flood of volcanic mud and gas that cooled around everything like candle wax. It sealed the air out so completely that wood survived. Scrolls too — whole rolled-up books, still here, just waiting for someone clever enough to unroll them without them crumbling."

Isla turned slowly on the spot, working it through out loud like she always did when a puzzle was clicking into place. "So it's not that one town got lucky and one didn't. It's that two completely different kinds of burying happened, and each one *saved* a different kind of thing."

"That's exactly it," said the smoke, sounding pleased. "Ash saved bread and paint. Mud and gas saved wood and paper. Between the two towns, almost the whole of ordinary Roman life got locked away — just in two different kinds of boxes."

Isla grinned at the charred, perfect little door. "Two mysteries for the price of one eruption."

"Try not to sound quite so delighted about that," the smoke said, "but yes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Mysteries in Paint
chapters.text:
The last stop smelled like old plaster and candle smoke. A long room, walls covered floor to ceiling in paintings — people in deep red robes, figures mid-dance, a scene that looked like some kind of ceremony nobody had explained to Isla yet.

"This is the **Villa of the Mysteries**," said the smoke. "That's its actual name, which is either extremely helpful or extremely unhelpful, depending on how you look at it."

Isla studied the figures — one seemed to be reading from a scroll, another raised in mid-step, a mask held up like it meant something important. "What's it actually showing?" she asked.

"Nobody knows for certain," the smoke admitted. "Experts have guessed for years — maybe a ceremony for a bride, maybe something to do with a god, maybe both. The paint survived almost perfectly. The *meaning* didn't come with instructions."

Isla folded her arms, delighted rather than frustrated — this was precisely the kind of problem she liked best, the kind with no clean answer waiting at the back of the book. "So it's a two-thousand-year-old picture book," she said, "and we've lost the story that goes with it."

"Put better than most of the experts manage," said the smoke.

She stood in front of the central figure a long moment, turning her own private theory over — something about the scroll-reader being the one explaining the ceremony to everyone else, the way a guide might. She didn't say it out loud. Some mysteries you got to keep for yourself.

"Can I come back to this one someday?" she asked. "For real. With my own eyes, not smoke."

"I'd bet on it," said the smoke.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain That Watches
chapters.text:
The last fold of smoke set her down somewhere bright and ordinary — gravel paths, sunhats, a family taking a photo by a stone wall, a guide holding up a little flag for a group to follow. Pompeii, but now, today.

"This is real-life now," Isla said, surprised by how steady the ground felt. "Like, actual tourists."

"Millions of them, every year," said the smoke. "It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site now — that just means a group of countries agreed it's so important that everyone should help look after it. One of the most-visited old places in all of Italy."

A woman in a wide hat crouched near a half-uncovered wall, brushing dust away in small careful strokes, a notebook open beside her.

"She's not finished," Isla realized. "There's still more town under there."

"About two-thirds of Pompeii has been dug up so far," said the smoke. "The rest is still waiting. New paintings turn up all the time — walls nobody's seen in almost two thousand years, uncovered for the very first time, last month, last year, probably next week too."

Far off, the mountain itself sat green and quiet against the sky, looking nothing like the thing that had done all this.

"Is it still... a volcano-volcano?" Isla asked. "Like, could it still—"

"It's still active," the smoke said. "Scientists called **volcanologists** — people whose whole job is understanding what volcanoes are doing underneath — watch it all the time, because so many people live close by today. It's not a sleeping secret. It's a mountain with its own research team."

Isla watched the woman with the brush work one more careful inch of wall into the daylight, and thought that was, in its own quiet way, exactly as brave as sailing a ship toward smoke. "Everyone down there's basically still finishing the story," she said.

"Every single day," the smoke agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The smoke drew back into the little lamp like water running downhill, and Isla was sitting cross-legged on her bedroom floor again, shoeboxes all around her exactly as she'd left them.

The lamp sat warm in her palms, the worn letters still faintly visible under her thumb. It smelled, very faintly, of salt and old ash.

She picked up her pen and opened a fresh page in her notebook. At the top she wrote FIND #23, and under it: *Small clay lamp. One town, buried twice over — once by a mountain, once by time. Rediscovered on purpose by people who kept looking.*

She set the lamp carefully on her shelf, right where she'd see it first thing in the morning, next to the bent key that was still, officially, unsolved.

Tomorrow there was a whole shoebox of mysteries left to get through.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Backyard Rainbow
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sunbeam, and a very colorful guide

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Backyard Rainbow
chapters.text:
Priya was drawing a lopsided dragon on the carpet. Dev snuck up with his water pistol. "SPLOOSH!" He missed her completely and soaked her sock instead.

But the spray flew right through a sunbeam from the window. Tiny stripes of color flickered in the mist.

"Whoa," said Priya, dropping her pencil.

The colors swirled and popped into a small glowing shape with a striped scarf. "Hiya! I'm Ray," it said, waving. "You two made a rainbow! The sun has to be behind you, and water in front of you. That's the whole trick."

Dev checked his pistol like it had superpowers. "I did that? With squirting?!"

"Every squirt's a little work of art," Ray said, winking at Priya's dragon. "Fancy a closer look?" The stripes stretched wide like a doorway, and in they went.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bending Light
chapters.text:
"Why do raindrops even make colors?" Priya asked, poking a floating droplet.

"Great question," said Ray. "Light zooms fast through air. But when it hits water, it slows down and bends, kind of like a bike wheel turning when it hits mud. That bending has a name: refraction."

Dev scrunched his nose. "Re-frac-shun?"

"Just means light bends," Ray said. "And here's the wild part: sunlight looks white, but it's actually every color mixed together."

Priya's jaw dropped. "Like all my markers squished into one?"

"Exactly like that," Ray said. "Each color bends a tiny bit differently, so inside the raindrop, they spread apart."

Dev tried bending his own arm like light. He wobbled and fell over. Everyone laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Roy G. Biv's Order
chapters.text:
A jumble of colors drifted past, all mixed up. "Hey, they're in the wrong order!" Priya said, pointing at her sketchbook. She'd drawn her rainbow with blue on the outside.

"Sharp eyes," said Ray. "Real rainbows always go the same way: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and two more — indigo and violet. People remember it with a name: Roy G. Biv."

"Roy Jee Biv," Dev repeated, giggling at the funny name.

"Red sits on the outside," Ray added, "because it bends the least. Violet bends the most, so it tucks in on the inside."

Priya grabbed her pencil and swapped the colors on her dragon's rainbow. "Better?" she asked.

"Picture perfect," said Ray.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Whole Circle
chapters.text:
Ray floated them up above the mist. "Did you know a rainbow is actually a full circle?"

Dev squinted. "But rainbows are just arcs, like a smile."

"Right — because the ground is in the way," Ray explained. "It blocks the bottom half."

"What if there was no ground?" Priya asked.

"Smart thinking," said Ray. "From an airplane, with no ground below you, people sometimes see the whole circle, like a colorful hula hoop in the sky."

Dev spun around with his arms out, pretending to be a flying hula-hoop rainbow. He bonked straight into a pillow-shaped cloud. Soft landing, big laugh.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Your Very Own Rainbow
chapters.text:
"Hey, your rainbow looks different from mine," Dev said, standing one step away from Priya.

Ray nodded. "That's because everybody actually sees their very own rainbow. It depends exactly where your eyes are standing."

Priya frowned, then grinned. "So nobody's ever seen the same rainbow as me? Not even you, Dev?"

"Nope!" said Ray. "You're each catching the light at your own angle."

Dev puffed up proudly. "I have a rainbow nobody else has ever seen. That's basically famous."

Priya rolled her eyes, laughing. "Famous for standing in one spot, maybe."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Twin Rainbow
chapters.text:
A fainter stripe glowed above the first one. "Look — a second rainbow!" Priya shouted, pointing up.

"Sharp eyes again," said Ray. "Sometimes light bounces twice inside the drops, and a second, fainter rainbow shows up above the first."

Dev squinted. "Why's it all backwards?"

"Because of that second bounce," Ray said, "the colors flip. Red ends up on the inside this time."

Priya compared the two rainbows with her fingers, tracing each color in order. "Matching bookends," she said.

Ray clapped. "Best way I've ever heard anyone put it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows in Strange Places
chapters.text:
Ray zipped them past a waterfall, spray flying everywhere. "Rainbows don't need rain clouds," Ray said. "They can show up in waterfall mist, garden hoses, even plain old fog."

Dev lifted his water pistol high and squeezed the trigger into a sunbeam. A tiny stripe of color flickered across the spray.

"Even in squirting," Ray laughed. "There's one more kind — a moonbow, made by moonlight instead of sunshine. It's usually so faint it just looks white or gray to our eyes, though cameras can catch its colors."

"A nighttime rainbow," Priya whispered. "That's kind of magical."

"Kind of," Ray agreed, "and kind of just light, doing its usual trick."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Old Stories and a Glass Trick
chapters.text:
"People have wondered about rainbows for a long time," Ray said, as old pictures floated by. "A scientist named Isaac Newton once took a triangle of glass, called a prism, and shone sunlight through it. Out came every single rainbow color."

"So he proved sunlight hides all the colors?" Priya asked.

"Back in the 1660s, yes," Ray said. "Old stories have fun ideas too. Norse tales call a rainbow Bifrost, a bridge to where the gods lived. In the Bible, a rainbow shows up as a gentle promise after a big storm had passed. And in Irish stories, folks say there's a pot of gold at a rainbow's end."

Dev's eyes went huge. "Gold?! Let's go find it!"

"Can't be done," Ray said gently. "A rainbow moves whenever you move, so you can never walk right up to one, or touch it. That part's just a nice old tale."

Dev slumped, then shrugged. "Fine. I'll just keep my water pistol."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Bedroom
chapters.text:
The colors folded closed like a storybook, and the carpet appeared beneath their feet again.

Dev looked down at his water pistol, now sparkling faintly. "Does it still work?"

Priya picked up her sketchbook. Her dragon now wore a perfect rainbow, red on the outside, violet tucked inside. "Ray's gonna love this," she said.

A last little shimmer blinked across the page, like a wink, then faded.

Dev squeezed his pistol toward the window, just to check. A tiny stripe of color flickered in the sunbeam for one second, then vanished.

"Still works," he grinned.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Seven colors, one light — sleep tight.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Shell That Opened the Sea
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Shell That Glowed
chapters.text:
Jack belly-flopped off his bed, goggles on. "CANNONBALL!" he yelled into his blanket ocean.

Ellie sat on the rug. She brushed her mermaid doll's hair and hummed a little tune.

Then the seashell nightlight on the shelf changed. It stopped glowing soft yellow. It flicked to green and began to hum, low and deep, like a whale far away.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "It never did that before."

Jack crept over. He poked the shell with one finger. It buzzed, warm as bathwater.

"What if it's trying to say something?" he said. He scooped it up in both hands.

The room filled with blue light. The floor tipped like a wave.

WHOOOOSH.

When the light cleared, they stood in water that stretched on forever. It looked dim and old, long before anyone built a house or a school. A shadow slid past, long and quiet. Ellie grabbed Jack's sleeve.

"It's okay," said a bubbly little voice. It was the shell, glowing softly in Jack's hands. "That's just an early shark. Sharks have swum in the sea for more than **400 million years**. That's so long ago, there weren't even dinosaurs yet. Or trees."

Jack watched the shadow bend and curve as it swam. "Its body looks so... bendy."

"Good eye," said the shell. "A shark's skeleton isn't hard bone like yours. It's made of **cartilage** — the same bendy stuff as the squishy part of your ear."

Jack grabbed his own ear and wiggled it. "Whoa. Bendy bones!"

"You kind of already have some," said the shell. "That's why your ears don't stay folded."

"Race you to the next one," Ellie called, already swimming off. The ocean swept them along behind her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow fell over them, huge and slow. It blocked out the light.

Ellie gasped and grabbed Jack's hand. Then the shadow opened its mouth, wide as a garage door. Nothing scary happened at all.

"That's a **whale shark**," said the shell. "It's the biggest fish in the whole world. Over **40 feet long**. But don't worry — it only eats **plankton**. Tiny bits of food floating in the water. Way too small to bother you."

Jack floated on his back, staring up at its enormous belly sliding by. "It's like swimming under a cloud," he said.

Jack counted the pale spots on its back, like stars on a dark blue sky. "One, two, three, four..." He lost count at twenty.

"Nobody's ever finished counting those," said the shell. "But some whale sharks live past **100 years old**. This one might be older than your great-great-grandpa."

Ellie reached out her hand, then remembered. She waved instead. "Hi, old fish."

The whale shark gave a slow flick of its tail and glided on, gentle as a cloud. Ellie floated after it a little way, humming her mermaid tune like a lullaby.

"It's bigger than our whole house," Ellie said, "and it just wants snacks."

"Most of the biggest things in the ocean," said the shell, "turn out to be the gentlest."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Teeth and Sandpaper Skin
chapters.text:
Jack's foot bumped something hard in the sand. He dug it up with both hands.

It was a tooth. Bigger than his whole hand. Curved and pointed like a knife made of bone.

"Whoa!" Jack held it up. "Whose tooth is THIS?"

"That belonged to **megalodon**," said the shell. "A giant shark that's **extinct** now. That means none are left alive, anywhere. It lived millions of years ago. Its teeth were as long as a human hand."

"How do we even know about it, if it's gone?" Jack asked.

"Teeth turn into **fossils**," said the shell. "They go hard like rock and last a very long time. Almost everything we know about megalodon comes from teeth just like that one."

Just then, a shark swimming nearby opened its mouth. A worn old tooth drifted loose and sank. A fresh new one slid forward to take its place.

"TOOTH SWAP!" Jack yelled.

"Sharks grow thousands of teeth in a lifetime," said the shell. "New ones keep moving up front. Like a conveyor belt."

Ellie reached out and gently ran her fingers along the shark's side as it passed. "It feels like sandpaper!"

"Tiny tooth-shaped bumps cover its skin," said the shell. "They help it swim smoothly. And yes — they're scratchy."

"Sharks," Jack announced, "are basically made of teeth."

"Pretty much," laughed the shell.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Hammer-Headed Hunter
chapters.text:
A strange shadow drifted close. It was shaped like a hammer, with eyes on each end.

"What happened to its head?" Ellie whispered.

"Nothing happened," said the shell. "That's just how a **hammerhead shark** grows. Its head is wide and flat. Its eyes sit far apart. It can see almost all the way around itself."

Jack watched it swing its head slowly side to side over the sand. "What's it doing?"

"Looking for dinner," said the shell. "Not just with its eyes. It's got jelly-filled bumps on its nose. They feel tiny electric sparks, even from a fish hiding under the sand."

Ellie spotted a lump in the sand and pointed. "Is something under there?"

The hammerhead swung its head straight at the spot. A little fish darted out and away.

"Found it," said the shell. "Nice call, Ellie."

"It didn't even need to see it!" Ellie said. "That's like a superpower."

Jack tried swinging his own head side to side, copying the shark. He got dizzy and flopped backward into the sand. Ellie laughed so hard bubbles came out her nose.

"Better than X-ray vision," Jack said, spitting out sand. "I'm never doing that again."

Ellie just kept giggling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Walking Shark and the Sleepy Shark
chapters.text:
Jack pointed at the reef. "Is that shark... walking?"

A small spotted shark used its fins like little paddle feet, scrambling over the coral.

"That's an **epaulette shark**," said the shell. "It can walk across reefs and puddles. It can even go hours without much air."

"I want fin-feet too," Jack said, eyeing his own hands.

"My turn!" He tried it anyway. He pushed along the sandy bottom with his hands like paddles. He sank nose-first into the sand instead, and came up sputtering with a crab stuck to his goggles.

Ellie giggled so hard she got the hiccups.

Further along, they found a shark lying totally still on the sea floor.

"Is it... okay?" Ellie whispered, worried.

"It's just resting," said the shell. "A **nurse shark** can pump water over its own gills while it lies still. Most sharks have to keep swimming to breathe. Not this one."

Ellie tiptoed close. She didn't touch it, just watched, and gave a tiny wave. "Shh. Sleeping shark."

"Good job remembering," said the shell. "Look, don't touch. Even with the sleepy ones."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Mermaid's Purses
chapters.text:
Something leathery and black drifted past. It was curled at the corners, like a little pillow.

Ellie caught it gently in both hands. "Is this... a real mermaid's purse?"

It was tough like a leather shoe, but soft at the edges.

"Close enough," said the shell. "That's what people call a shark egg case. Some sharks lay their babies inside cases just like that one. Other sharks just have live babies, like puppies."

Ellie peered at it, turning it over. "Does it have a window?"

"No window," laughed the shell. "But you can imagine a tiny shark curled up inside. Just like a chick in an egg."

Ellie hugged it to her chest. "I'm keeping this one safe."

A streak of silver shot past so fast it left bubbles swirling behind.

"That," said the shell, "was a **shortfin mako**. The fastest shark there is."

"Race you!" Jack shouted. He kicked off after it, goggles fogging, arms flailing — and lost, badly, before it vanished into the blue.

"Worth a try," he panted.

"Some sharks, like the **bull shark**, can swim in rivers too," the shell added. "Not just the sea. They've been found a long way from the ocean."

"A shark... in a river?" Jack blinked. "That seems like cheating."

"Sharks," said the shell, "are full of surprises."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A diver glided toward them, smiling behind her mask. Sharks swam easily all around her, like she was an old friend.

"Hello," she said. "I'm **Eugenie Clark**. People call me the Shark Lady."

"You're not scared of them?" Ellie asked.

"Not one bit," said Eugenie. "I spent years studying sharks. I even trained some to push buttons for their food. Sharks are curious. They can learn, just like a dog can."

Jack frowned, thinking hard. "But... sharks bite people. Don't they?"

"Almost never," said Eugenie. "Shark bites on people are very rare. Honestly, people have hurt far more sharks than sharks have ever hurt us. These days, lots of people are working hard to keep sharks safe instead."

"Why do we even need sharks?" Ellie asked.

"They sit at the very top of the ocean's food chain," said Eugenie. "That's called being an **apex predator** — eating others, but hardly ever getting eaten. They keep everything else in the sea balanced. No sharks, and the whole ocean gets wobbly."

"There are more than **500 different kinds** of shark swimming around today," added the shell, popping up beside them. "And you two have just met a few of the best."

Jack looked out at the glowing blue water. "When I grow up," he said, "I want to study sharks. Like you."

Eugenie smiled. "The ocean could always use another shark scientist."

"Me too!" said Ellie. "But I'm also keeping my mermaid's purse."

Eugenie laughed. "Fair enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
The shell in Jack's hands began to pulse. Slower and slower, like it was getting sleepy too.

"Time to go home," it said gently.

Ellie squeezed her mermaid's purse one last time. Then she let it drift back down into the blue. "Bye, little egg."

The water filled with blue light again. The floor tipped.

WHOOOOSH.

They landed with a soft thump. Back on the bedroom carpet, blanket ocean and all.

The nightlight on the shelf glowed its usual soft yellow. It hummed once, then stopped.

But on the carpet between them sat something new. A small, smooth, white shape, curved and pointed, about the size of Jack's thumb.

"Is that..." Jack picked it up, turning it over. "A tiny tooth! A souvenir!"

Jack held it up to the nightlight's soft glow. "Thanks for the trip," he whispered to the shell. It gave one last gentle pulse, almost like a wink.

Ellie yawned a huge yawn. She flopped back onto her pillow, mermaid doll tucked under one arm.

"Goodnight, sharks," she mumbled. "Goodnight, mermaid's purses."

Jack set the little tooth on his nightstand, right next to his goggles. Then he climbed into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Dive deep, and dream well.

story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Express
story.subtitle: A gentle night ride through why we sleep

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Owl
chapters.text:
Leo loved trains. He loved owls even more.

Leo lined up his wooden trains on the floor. CHUFF, CHUFF, his blue engine rolled past his bed.

On his shelf, Ollie the owl nightlight blinked. His round eyes glowed soft and gold.

"Hello, Leo," said Ollie. "Want to see where sleep comes from?"

Leo looked at his dark window. "Is it scary?" he asked.

Ollie gave a soft hoot. "No dark here. Just stars, and me." He spread his wings. They turned into train doors.

WHOOSH! A shiny night train rolled right into Leo's room. Leo grinned and hopped aboard. The Sleepy Express was leaving.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Twitchy Eyes
chapters.text:
The train stopped in an old, quiet room. A kind scientist named Nathaniel Kleitman watched a sleeping boy.

Another scientist, Eugene Aserinsky, leaned close. "Look," he whispered. "His eyes are moving!"

Leo peeked too. Under the boy's closed eyelids, his eyes flicked side to side. Leo pointed. "He's watching something in his dream!"

"Good eye, Leo," said Kleitman. "In **1953**, we found this dreaming sleep. We call it **REM sleep**. It means the eyes move fast while you dream."

"Exactly," said Ollie. "You just helped make history."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Loop-the-Loop Track
chapters.text:
Next, the train rolled onto a big looping track, round and round.

"This is like your sleep," said Ollie. "Every night, your sleep goes in loops too, about **ninety minutes** each."

"Like my train going round my room?" Leo asked.

"Just like that," said Ollie. "First comes quiet, still sleep. Then comes dream sleep, when your eyes dance. Then quiet again, all night long."

Leo watched his toy train loop past three times. "One, two, three bedtimes in one night!"

"And in the deepest, quietest part," said Ollie, "your body makes a **growing helper**, so you grow bigger and stronger."

"I want to grow super big!" said Leo.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Floppy Rag Doll
chapters.text:
The train chugged past a cozy cabin. Inside, a child slept, arms soft and floppy like a rag doll.

"During dream sleep," said Ollie, "your brain is busy, almost like when you're awake."

"Then why don't they jump out of bed?" Leo asked.

"Good question," said Ollie. "Your muscles go **floppy**, so your body stays still and safe while your brain dreams."

Leo flopped his own arms like noodles. "Floppy like this?"

"Just like that," Ollie laughed. "So you never act out your dream adventures."

Leo giggled and flopped again, a happy sleepy noodle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tiny Clock
chapters.text:
The train slowed by a tiny glowing dot, right behind Leo's own eyes.

"That little spot," said Ollie, "is a clock inside your brain. It tells your body when to sleep and when to wake."

Leo tapped his forehead. "A clock in here?"

"Tucked in tight," said Ollie. "It keeps you on schedule, all by itself, even in the dark."

Leo smiled. "So the dark just means my clock says sleepy time."

"Exactly," said Ollie. "Nothing scary. Just your clock, doing its job."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Potion
chapters.text:
Next stop: a tiny lab with bubbling jars.

"In **1958**," said Ollie, "a scientist named Aaron Lerner found a sleepy potion inside bodies. We call it **melatonin**. It whispers, 'time for bed,' when it gets dark."

Leo yawned. "I think mine is whispering right now."

"Sounds like it," Ollie chuckled. "That potion only comes out in the dark. Dark isn't scary. Dark just means your bedtime potion is turning on."

Leo yawned again, even bigger.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleepy Animal Parade
chapters.text:
The train rolled through a sleepy jungle.

"Look," said Ollie. A dolphin swam by with one eye open. "Dolphins sleep with half their brain awake, so they can still watch for danger."

A giraffe dozed nearby, just for a moment. "Giraffes barely nap," said Ollie, "sometimes **under two hours** a day!"

A tiny bat hung upside down, snoozing away. "This little bat," Ollie said, "sleeps up to **twenty hours** a day."

"And newborn babies," Ollie added, "sleep almost all day too, up to **seventeen hours**."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Ride Home
chapters.text:
"One more thing," said Ollie. "Sleep helps your brain tidy up your whole day, like putting toys back in their boxes. That's how you remember things you practiced, like your train tracks."

"So sleep helps me remember stuff?" Leo asked.

"Exactly," said Ollie. "That's why sleep matters so much. A boy named Randy once stayed awake a very long time, just to see what would happen. It taught scientists a lot, but doctors say nobody should ever try that. Sleep is too important to skip."

The train looped back home, gentle as a lullaby. Leo climbed into bed. Ollie glowed soft gold on the shelf, humming a tiny engine song. Leo smiled, snug in his blanket.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Sleep tight, and play well.
