fact_pack.summary: Every person and almost every animal sleeps, though scientists still study exactly why. Sleep runs in repeating brain cycles that help the body grow, heal, and sort memories.

facts.text: In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.
A night's sleep is made of repeating cycles about 90 minutes long, moving between quiet non-REM sleep and active, dream-filled REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go limp so the sleeper cannot act out dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage triggers the most growth hormone release, one reason growing children need extra sleep.
A tiny brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
'Circadian,' the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone melatonin was first isolated in 1958 by scientist Aaron Lerner's team, extracted from animal pineal glands.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so good sleep can help someone remember what they practiced or learned.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the glymphatic system flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.
In 1964, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner of San Diego stayed awake about eleven days for a science-fair project, one of the longest documented periods without sleep.
Doctors do not recommend anyone try to break sleep-deprivation records, since going without sleep quickly harms mood, attention, and memory.
Newborns sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day in short bursts, nearly half of it in REM sleep.
Bottlenose dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming.
Giraffes are among the shortest sleepers of any large mammal, sometimes under two hours a day in brief standing naps.
Some small bats sleep up to 20 hours a day, making them among the sleepiest mammals known.
Sleepwalking happens during deep non-REM sleep, not during dreaming, so sleepwalkers are usually not acting out a dream.
People spend roughly a third of their life asleep, based on typical nightly totals over a lifetime.
Nathaniel Kleitman, co-discoverer of REM sleep, is often called the father of modern sleep research.
In 1899, Sigmund Freud published 'The Interpretation of Dreams,' arguing dreams reveal hidden wishes; most of this specific theory is not accepted by scientists today.
Even fruit flies show sleep-like rest states, suggesting sleep is extremely ancient in life's history.
Chronic short sleep over months or years is linked by health researchers to problems with mood, learning, and the body's ability to fight illness.

story.title: Arjun and the Nightwatchman of Sleep
story.subtitle: A ninety-minute tour through why bodies need to rest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Flashlight Under the Blanket
chapters.text:
Arjun was five minutes into his five more minutes. Again.

His flashlight beam wobbled over the last panel of *Captain Click*, where the hero's mask always had one eye half-shut, mid-wink. Tonight the eye blinked. On its own. Then it flicked sideways, left, right, left, fast as a bee.

Arjun sat bolt upright. The panel peeled off the page like a sticker, and a man in cricket pads and a cape made of bat-grip tape stepped onto the carpet.

"Name's the Nightwatchman," he said, straightening a helmet with a crescent moon on it. "You caught my eyes twitching. Good eye. Want to know why?"

Arjun, forgetting he was meant to be asleep, nodded hard.

"Back in **1953**, two scientists at the **University of Chicago** - **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** - watched a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids, just like mine," said the Nightwatchman. "That twitchy kind of sleep got a name: **REM**, short for Rapid Eye Movement. They were the first to spot it properly."

"So you're doing REM right now?"

"Every night. So is everybody. Fancy a look inside one?"

Arjun grabbed his bat from beside the bed, because obviously you take your bat everywhere, and the room folded into green light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ninety-Minute Pitch
chapters.text:
They landed on a pitch under floodlights that pulsed slow, like a heartbeat.

"Sleep isn't one long nap," said the Nightwatchman. "It's **cycles**, about **ninety minutes** each, back and forth between quiet sleep and twitchy REM sleep, all night long."

Arjun counted the floodlight pulses. Fast-slow, fast-slow. "That's like session breaks in a Test match," he said. "Quiet overs, then a flurry, then quiet again."

"Good comparison," said the Nightwatchman, and bowed, pads clanking.

Mid-pitch, a kid-shaped shadow wandered past, eyes shut, perfectly steady, stepping around the stumps without knocking one.

"Sleepwalker," the Nightwatchman explained. "That happens in deep, quiet sleep, not during dreaming. So he's not acting out a dream. Just a very calm stroll."

Then the Nightwatchman flopped sideways onto the grass, completely boneless, like a puppet with its strings cut.

"During REM," he said, muffled, from the ground, "the brain's as busy as if you were awake. But the muscles go **limp**. Nobody can act out their dreams. Handy, really."

Arjun poked him with the bat. Nothing. "You're basically a beanbag."

"A very dignified beanbag," the Nightwatchman agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Growing Stadium
chapters.text:
Next the stands around them seemed to stretch upward, brick by brick, like a stadium rising overnight.

"Deepest, quietest sleep," said the Nightwatchman, "is when the body lets loose the most **growth hormone** - the stuff that helps kids like you grow taller."

Arjun stood very straight. "Does that mean if I sleep more, I'll be tall enough to open the batting for the school team?"

"Can't promise you anyone's height by Tuesday. But skipping sleep definitely won't help."

Arjun found a wall marked with chalk lines, one for every year. He measured himself, worried for a second he'd shrunk, then realized last year's mark was from before his growth spurt. He was taller after all.

He added today's mark himself, a full inch higher, and grinned.

"Turns out," he said, "I grew. While I was asleep."

"Exactly where it happens," said the Nightwatchman.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Clock Tower Above the Stumps
chapters.text:
A clock tower stood at the edge of the stadium, its face glowing soft blue.

"Every body has a clock like this," said the Nightwatchman, "a tiny speck of brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, sitting right where your eye nerves cross. It's the body's master clock for sleeping and waking."

Arjun squinted at a brass plate on the tower: CIRCA + DIES.

"Circa... about. Dies... day," he read slowly, picking up bits of Latin from comic captions. "About a day?"

"**Circadian** means exactly that," said the Nightwatchman. "Your clock isn't a perfect twenty-four hours. It's *about* a day."

Deep inside the tower, gears turned - and one gear, tiny and golden, was stuck.

Arjun reached in and gave it a nudge. It clicked into place, and the whole tower hummed back to life.

"In **2017**," said the Nightwatchman, "three scientists - **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** - won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that keep that clock ticking. Built from tiny moving parts, it turns out."

"I fixed a Nobel Prize gear," said Arjun. "With my thumb."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Dimmer Switch
chapters.text:
Past the tower stood a lamp as tall as a sightscreen, its bulb impossibly bright.

"Turn it down," said the Nightwatchman, "and your brain makes something called **melatonin** - a sleepy-time hormone that tells your body it's bedtime."

"A chemical just for being sleepy?"

"Found in **1958**, by a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team. Pulled it straight out of a gland the size of a pea."

Arjun reached for the dimmer switch himself and turned it slowly. The light dropped from stadium-floodlight white to streetlamp orange to almost nothing.

As it dimmed, the Nightwatchman's shoulders drooped, his eyelids sagged, his words slowed right... down.

"See?" he mumbled. "Dark... makes... the... melatonin..."

Arjun turned the dimmer back up a notch so the Nightwatchman wouldn't fall asleep mid-sentence and leave him stranded.

"Cheers," said the Nightwatchman, snapping upright. "Nearly lost me there."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Memory Vault
chapters.text:
Behind a stumps-shaped door sat a vault stacked with glowing panels - each one a memory.

"Sleep sorts these," said the Nightwatchman, "into long-term memory. That late cut you practiced all week? Sleep's the thing that helps it stick."

Arjun spotted a panel of himself missing a catch yesterday, and another, weeks back, of him nailing one, right after a good night's sleep.

"So if I sleep tonight," Arjun said, "tomorrow's practice might actually work?"

"That's the idea."

A soft whooshing came from pipes along the vault's ceiling.

"That's the **glymphatic system**," said the Nightwatchman, "a nightly rinse that washes waste out of a sleeping brain. Like a dishwasher that only runs at night."

"My brain has a dishwasher."

"Everyone's does. Running right now, if you'd let it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Animal Awards Booth
chapters.text:
A booth popped up, strung with comic-style trading cards.

"**Bottlenose dolphins**, and some seals," the Nightwatchman read off one card, "sleep with only half their brain at a time. One eye stays open, watching for danger, or keeping them swimming."

Arjun flipped the next card. A giraffe, legs still standing. "Giraffes barely sleep? Sometimes under two hours a day, in little naps, standing up?"

"Among the shortest sleepers of any big animal," confirmed the Nightwatchman.

One more card: a tiny bat, curled up tight. "Some small bats sleep up to **twenty hours** a day. Practically professionals."

Arjun studied the cards, then picked his favorite - not the giraffe, who barely rested, and not the show-off bat, but the dolphin, half-awake, half-dreaming, still watching the world.

"That one's basically me during a boring lesson," said Arjun.

The Nightwatchman laughed so hard his cape fluttered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Wide-Awake Record
chapters.text:
A giant scoreboard glowed at the pitch's far end: LONGEST AWAKE.

"In **1964**, a seventeen-year-old named **Randy Gardner**, from **San Diego**, stayed awake about **eleven days** straight. For a science-fair project."

Arjun's eyes went wide. "Eleven days? That's basically my dream record. Five more minutes, times infinity."

"Don't get any ideas," said the Nightwatchman firmly. "Doctors don't recommend anyone try to beat that. Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your attention, your memory - fast."

Arjun thought about the panel of himself dropping a catch, tired. He thought about the chalk mark, an inch higher.

"Yeah," he said. "I'll pass on the record."

The scoreboard, and the stadium, and the Nightwatchman, folded gently back into a comic panel, which folded back into the last page of *Captain Click*.

Arjun was back under his blanket, flashlight dim, comic closed on his chest.

On the final panel, the hero's eye had stopped twitching. Shut, peacefully, mid-wink, same as always - except now a tiny cricket bat leaned against the panel's corner, where it hadn't been before.

Arjun clicked off the flashlight. No five more minutes tonight.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a catch to practice, and sleep, it turned out, was most of the training.

story.title: Noah and the Ninety-Minute Loop
story.subtitle: A midnight tour through the science of sleep, hosted by a DJ who never sleeps at all

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The 2:47 A.M. Shuffle
chapters.text:
Noah was not supposed to be awake. The clock on his nightstand said **2:47 A.M.**, which meant he had been scrolling through music for exactly three hours and forty minutes longer than he meant to.

His playlist shuffled to a track he didn't recognize: **"REM Cycle — 90 Min Loop."** The album art was a single eye, mid-blink. He tapped it out of pure curiosity, which is the thing that gets thirteen-year-olds into most of their best trouble.

The screen didn't play music. It turned static-green and a figure folded itself out of the light — somewhere between a DJ and a desk lamp, with two turntables for shoulders. "Delta," it said, extending a hand made of equalizer bars. "I mix brainwaves. You're about to learn why you're terrible at falling asleep on time."

"I'm good at it," Noah said. "I just do it at 4 A.M. instead of ten."

"That," said Delta, "is exactly the problem we're going to fix."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boy Whose Eyes Wouldn't Stay Still
chapters.text:
Delta pulled up a black-and-white memory like it was scrubbing a track. A small lab, a sleeping kid, two scientists hunched over him with wires taped near his eyes.

"**1953**, University of Chicago," Delta said. "**Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** were watching a boy sleep when his eyes started twitching back and forth under his eyelids — fast, like he was watching a tennis match in his dreams. They'd just found **REM sleep**, the stage where your eyes move even though the rest of you is out cold."

Noah squinted at the eye on the hologram. "Wait — so before 1953 nobody knew dreaming had its own mode?"

"Nobody had proven it," Delta said. "Kleitman spent so much of his life studying sleep that people still call him the father of the whole field. Not a bad title for a guy who basically got paid to watch people nap."

"I could do that job," Noah said. "I'm extremely qualified."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ninety-Minute Playlist
chapters.text:
Delta spun a dial and a glowing waveform unrolled across the floor like a setlist — peaks and valleys, over and over, evenly spaced.

"Look at the spacing," Delta said. "What do you notice?"

Noah traced the gaps with his finger. "They repeat. Like... every track's the same length?"

"Close. A full sleep cycle runs about **90 minutes**, bouncing between quiet, deep **non-REM sleep** and the busier, dreamier **REM sleep**, then starting over. You run through several of these loops a night, like an album on repeat."

"So when my alarm goes off and I feel like garbage," Noah said, "it's because it caught me mid-track instead of between songs?"

"Exactly," Delta said. "You just explained sleep science better than most textbooks. Try not to let it go to your head — you still need the next nine hours to actually work."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Controller Unplugs Itself
chapters.text:
The waveform shifted into a bright, jagged peak. "REM," Delta announced. "Your brain here is almost as busy as when you're awake — scanning, sorting, basically running a full session."

"So I'm basically gaming in my sleep," Noah said.

"Sort of. Except your body pulls the plug on your muscles. They go completely limp during REM, so you can't actually act out whatever wild thing you're dreaming about."

Noah frowned. "My body benches itself on purpose?"

"On purpose. Imagine if it didn't — every dream where you're dodging something would end with you falling out of bed." Delta paused. "Some people do kick a little. Nobody said the system's perfect."

"Controller unplugged mid-match," Noah said. "That's actually a genius failsafe."

"Your body thought of it a few hundred thousand years before you did," said Delta.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Growth Patch
chapters.text:
The waveform dipped into its deepest, slowest valley. "This," Delta said, "is the deep stage of non-REM. It's where your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the stuff that pushes your body to grow and repair itself."

Noah glanced down at his own arms, which had recently and alarmingly outgrown two hoodies. "So this is basically the update patch."

"Basically. Skip it enough nights and the patch doesn't fully install. You just stay buggy."

"I'm not buggy," Noah said. "I'm in beta."

"Everyone your age is in beta," Delta said. "That's why you need more of this stage than I do. I don't even have a body. I'm a lighting rig with opinions."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Master Clock
chapters.text:
Delta zoomed in on a tiny cluster of light, tucked just behind the hologram's eyes. "This is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — a pinch of brain sitting right where your eye nerves cross. Think of it as your body's master clock."

"That's a lot of syllables for a clock," Noah said.

"The whole system is called **circadian**, from Latin words meaning roughly 'about a day' — because this clock keeps your body on a loop close to **24 hours**, telling it when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake."

"Like a server tick rate," Noah said. "Keeps everything synced."

"Keep going. In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash,** and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that make that clock tick. Decades of work, just to prove your body runs on a schedule."

"And I override mine nightly with my phone," Noah said. "Rude of me."

"Extremely rude," Delta agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Night Mode, Then and Now
chapters.text:
Delta tapped the glowing screen, and it flipped to a soft orange hue — Noah's own phone, mid-scroll, its night mode doing its usual thing.

"Your clock listens to a hormone called **melatonin**," Delta said. "It rises when it gets dark and tells your body it's bedtime. Scientists first pulled it out and studied it in **1958**, in **Aaron Lerner's** lab."

"And bright screens mess with that," Noah said. "I already know this lecture."

"Knowing it and acting on it are different sports. While you sleep, your brain also runs something called the **glymphatic system** — a nightly rinse cycle that flushes waste out of your brain like emptying a cache. And it sorts the day into memories, so whatever you practiced — guitar riffs, game strategies, whatever — actually sticks."

"So pulling an all-nighter before a test is—"

"Deleting the save file before it finishes writing," Delta said. "Yes."
chapters.shout_line: DELETING THE SAVE FILE BEFORE IT FINISHES WRITING.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Eleven Days and the Way Home
chapters.text:
Delta pulled up one last clip: a teenager, grinning, clearly exhausted, surrounded by reporters. "**Randy Gardner**, San Diego, **1964**. Seventeen years old. He stayed awake about **eleven days** for a school science project — one of the longest stretches on record."

"Eleven *days*?" Noah sat up. "That's insane. That's a legend."

"It's a real record, and also a terrible idea," Delta said. "Doctors don't want anyone trying to beat it — going without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory, fast. Cool story. Do not attempt."

Noah held up both hands. "Noted. I'll stick to four hours, not zero."

"Still not great," Delta said, "but we're making progress. Also — sleepwalkers aren't acting out dreams. Sleepwalking happens in deep non-REM, the quiet stage, not the dreaming one. People just assume the dramatic version." The waveform folded itself back into a single calm line. "People spend roughly a third of their whole lives asleep. It's not wasted time. It's maintenance."

The green light faded. Noah blinked, and he was back in his bed, phone dark on the nightstand, 2:51 A.M. glowing where 2:47 had been. Only four minutes had passed. His eyes, for once, felt heavy in the right way.

He set the phone face-down, which for Noah was basically a miracle.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow night, lights out before midnight. Probably.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: All aboard for beeps, boots, and one very big splash.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Porthole That Wasn't Water
chapters.text:
Maya was drawing a boat with a long paper sail, lying on her belly on the rug. It had been one whole week since the humming bridge finished, and her last rivet picture still hung crooked by her bed.

Tonight she found something new in the toy box: a round brass porthole, like a window from a ship. The glass looked wet, even though her fingers came away dry. She turned it over once. The glass went swirly, like water stirred by a spoon, and a whiskery nose poked right through.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, flopping half out of the glass. "Tonight we are not going under the sea. We are going up. Way, way up."

Behind him, the porthole showed black sky and one tiny silver ball, blinking.

"What is that beeping dot?" Maya asked, pressing her nose right up to the glass.

"That is Sputnik 1," said Barnacle. "On **October 4, 1957**, a country called the Soviet Union — Russia, back then — launched it into space. It was the very first thing people ever built to fly all the way around our Earth."

"It's tiny!" Maya said.

"About as wide as your beach ball," said Barnacle. "Just **58 centimeters** across. But it sent out a little radio beep, and people everywhere could hear it, on ordinary radios, like the one in your kitchen."

Maya traced the dot's path with her finger, round and round the little blue globe, slow and careful. "It goes all the way around and comes right back to the same spot!"

"That's called an orbit," said Barnacle. "Going around and around a planet, the way a boat sails around an island. You worked that out yourself, just now."

Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. Her finger had drawn a perfect circle on the glass. The porthole shivered, like it liked being traced, and the picture inside began to change.

"Where to next?" Maya asked, already bouncing on her knees.

"Follow the beep," said Barnacle, and dove back through the glass with a flick of his tail.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Surprised Country
chapters.text:
The porthole swirled and showed a room full of grown-ups hunched over newspapers, looking worried.

"Everybody in America was surprised," said Barnacle, "when that little beeping ball flew right over their houses. So they decided their country needed its own space team."

"Like a crew for a boat," said Maya.

"Just like that," said Barnacle. "On **October 1, 1958**, the United States started a brand-new team. It was just for space."

A plain grey rocket sat waiting on a launch pad, with nothing painted on its side.

"It needs a name," Maya said. She grabbed her pencil and wrote four big letters on a scrap of paper, then held it up to the glass: N-A-S-A.

"Good eye," laughed Barnacle. "That's exactly what they called it. NASA."

The rocket roared up, and the porthole showed a little satellite zooming past a faint glowing ring that circled Earth like a hula hoop left spinning in the sky.

"What's that stripe?" Maya asked, tapping the glass.

"That's Explorer 1, America's first satellite," said Barnacle. "It launched **January 31, 1958**. And it found something nobody even knew was there — a giant invisible ring of space weather, wrapped clear around our whole Earth. People named it the Van Allen belt, after the scientist who spotted it."

"I found the ring too," Maya said proudly, poking the glowing stripe. "I saw it before you said anything."

"You did," said Barnacle. "Good eyes run in this crew, Maya. Must be all that boat-watching."

Maya patted the glass right where the ring glowed, and it pulsed once, soft and warm, almost like it was waving back at her. She traced it twice more for luck.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Brave Passenger
chapters.text:
The glass swirled to show a small round rocket with a little window, and inside sat a small dog with perky, pointed ears.

"Who's that?" Maya asked, leaning so close her breath fogged the glass.

"Her name is Laika," said Barnacle, his voice going soft. "On **November 3, 1957**, she became the very first living creature to ever circle the Earth."

"She looks brave," Maya said.

"She was," said Barnacle. "The bravest kind of traveler — the first one, before anybody even knew what space would be like."

Maya pressed her hand flat on the glass, right over the little dog. "I hope she knew everybody back home was proud of her."

"I think she did," said Barnacle gently. "Dogs always know when they're loved. It's one of the best things about dogs."

"Can I draw her?" Maya asked. "So I remember her."

Barnacle nodded, and Maya sketched fast: two round ears, a small smiling snout, a window shaped like a circle around her.

"Best portrait I've seen all week," said Barnacle, peeking over with his whiskers tickling her arm.

Maya blew a tiny kiss at the glass, and the little dog's picture softly faded, like a wave pulling back from the sand, leaving a clean patch of sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Spin Around the World
chapters.text:
The next picture showed two round capsules side by side, one marked with red letters, one with white ones.

"Which one goes first?" Maya asked, hopping up onto her knees.

"Watch," said Barnacle.

The red capsule shot up first, flames roaring underneath it. "On **April 12, 1961**, Yuri Gagarin became the first human ever to fly in space," said Barnacle. "He rode a ship called Vostok 1, and he flew all the way around Earth once — about **108 minutes**, start to finish."

"That's less time than two cartoons!" Maya said, counting on her fingers.

"Exactly," laughed Barnacle. "Fast trip, big record."

Then the white capsule rose too — but this one didn't loop all the way around. It just arced up high and came straight back down.

"Why didn't that one go around?" Maya asked, squinting at the glass.

"Good question," said Barnacle. "That's Alan Shepard, the first American in space, on **May 5, 1961**. His ship was called Freedom 7. It went up and came right back down — no full circle that time."

Maya traced both paths in the air with her finger: one big looping circle, one small bump. "I get it now. One went all the way around the whole world. The other one just visited."

"You sorted that out faster than most grown-ups do," said Barnacle, clapping his flippers together, which mostly just made a soft, floppy sound since he has no hands at all.

Maya giggled so hard she nearly rolled right off the rug.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Moon Dare and the Factory Girl
chapters.text:
A man in a dark suit stood at a podium, pointing straight up at the sky.

"That's President Kennedy," said Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, he told his whole country something big: America would land a person on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before ten years were up."

Maya looked at the round white Moon hanging in the porthole's sky. "That's so far away."

"It is," agreed Barnacle. "But people love a good dare."

Maya grabbed her pencil and drew a tiny flag on a tiny moon, right on her scrap paper. "There. Now it's a goal. Like drawing a map of where you want to go."

"That's exactly how it started," said Barnacle.

The picture shifted to show a woman in a round space helmet, waving from a hatch with a big smile.

"Who's she?" Maya asked.

"Valentina Tereshkova," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory. Then, on **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, going around Earth aboard a ship called Vostok 6."

"From a factory to space," Maya said, eyes wide. "That's like jumping from the bathtub straight to the ocean."

"Big jumps happen," said Barnacle, "when somebody says yes to a dare."

Maya looked down at her little flag drawing and smiled. She folded it carefully and tucked it in her pocket, like something worth keeping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating and the Picture of Home
chapters.text:
The porthole swirled to show a puffy white-suited astronaut floating completely outside his ship, nothing but black space all around him.

"Is he swimming?" Maya gasped. "Like floating in the deep end!"

"Kind of," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, Alexei Leonov became the first person ever to float outside his own spacecraft. We call that a spacewalk."

"How long did he float?" Maya asked.

"Guess," said Barnacle. "Count it out slow."

Maya counted on her fingers, careful and steady. "One, two, three... all the way to ten?"

"Close enough," said Barnacle. "About **ten minutes**, out there with the whole universe around him."

Maya shivered, happily. "I'd want to float forever."

The scene changed: a small ship circling a grey, bumpy moon, and inside, an astronaut lifted a camera to the window.

"What's he taking a picture of?" Maya asked.

"Watch," said Barnacle.

The astronaut, a man named William Anders, snapped his camera — and there was Earth, blue and round and small, rising over the Moon's grey edge like a marble over a hill.

"In **December 1968**, the crew of Apollo 8 became the first people ever to orbit the Moon," said Barnacle. "That photo he just took got famous. People call it Earthrise."

Maya grabbed her pencil at once. "I want to draw that too." She drew a round blue dot rising above a grey bumpy line, careful and quick, tongue poking out the side of her mouth.

"Perfect copy," said Barnacle, peering over her shoulder.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A rocket taller than anything Maya had ever seen stood waiting on a launch pad, steam curling off its sides.

"How tall is that thing?" Maya asked, tipping her head all the way back.

"That's the Saturn V," said Barnacle. "It stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty. A man named Wernher von Braun led the team that designed it."

"That's taller than my whole street," Maya breathed.

On **July 20, 1969**, the rocket's crew reached the Moon. The porthole showed a ladder, and a boot stepping slowly down onto grey, dusty ground.

"Neil Armstrong," said Barnacle. "The first person ever to walk on the Moon. He said it was one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

"Who's that other astronaut bouncing around?" Maya asked, pointing at a second figure hopping across the dust like it was made of springs.

"That's Buzz Aldrin," said Barnacle. "He joined Armstrong down on the surface."

Maya counted the tiny bouncing figures. "That's only two. Wasn't there a third person?"

Barnacle grinned under his whiskers. "Sharp eyes, Maya. Michael Collins stayed up above, alone, flying around the Moon in the command ship — it was named Columbia — waiting for his friends to come back up."

"So he was like the one who stays with the boat," Maya said, "while everyone else explores the island."

"Precisely like that," said Barnacle.

Maya watched the two little figures bounce in the grey dust, light as balloons, and laughed out loud until her sides hurt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Splashing Home
chapters.text:
The porthole flickered, and the picture inside looked shakier this time, bumpier.

"In **1970**," said Barnacle, keeping his voice calm and gentle, "a tank on a ship called Apollo 13 broke, partway to the Moon. The whole ship shuddered."

Maya's stomach did a little flip. "Are they okay?"

"Watch what happens," said Barnacle.

People on the ground worked and worked, drawing diagrams, testing ideas, passing sketches back and forth, until they found a way to bring the ship safely home.

Maya remembered all the splashdowns she'd seen in the other pictures that night. "I bet they land in the ocean, like a boat," she said. "That's how all the other ones came home."

"Exactly right," said Barnacle. "And that's just what happened. The whole crew made it safely back to Earth."

The capsule dropped through clouds on big round parachutes and hit the water.

**SPLOOSH!**

Maya clapped both hands. "I knew it! Boats always come home."

The porthole swirled one last time, showing two spaceships — one marked with Soviet letters, one with American ones — slowly turning to meet each other against the black sky.

"On **July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle, "an American ship and a Soviet ship met up in space and locked together. The crews opened a hatch between them and shook hands, right there above the Earth. That was the end of the whole space race — not with a winner, but with a handshake."

"That's a nice way to finish a race," Maya said.

"The best way there is," agreed Barnacle.

The glass went calm and clear again, just an ordinary brass porthole. Maya looked down at her pile of drawings: a small brave dog, a blue Earth rising, two bouncing astronauts, a splash of white parachutes, one tiny flag on a tiny moon. "Same crew next time?" Barnacle asked, poking his nose through the glass one last time.

"Always," Maya said, yawning a huge yawn. "All aboard, Barnacle."

He winked, and slipped back beneath the glass, gone quiet and still, like water settling after a seal dives down deep.

story.title: Eli and the Signal from 1957
story.subtitle: A journey through the Space Race, one impossible radio station at a time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep That Wasn't Noise
chapters.text:
The smell of hot solder always meant one thing: Eli was deep inside Whisper again.

Whisper was his grandfather's old shortwave radio, a scarred wooden box of tubes and dials that hadn't worked in years. Eli had spent three weekends resurrecting it, tracing wires, testing capacitors, chasing a short circuit he could not find. Tonight he'd finally gotten the dial to glow — and the second it did, Whisper started beeping.

Not static. Not the hiss and crackle of dead air. A beep, then a gap, then the same beep again, over and over, dead even, like a metronome built by someone who never got bored.

Eli frowned at it the way he frowned at a problem set. Real noise wobbles. Lightning crackles unevenly, radio interference drifts. This beep did neither. The interval between pulses was constant to the second, which meant one thing in his physics brain: something was transmitting it on purpose, and whatever was doing the transmitting was moving in a perfect, repeating loop.

"That's not weather," he said out loud. "That's an orbit."

The dial flared white. The beeping swallowed the room, and the workbench dissolved into a sheet of cold light.

Eli landed in a field full of men hunched over radio sets that looked almost exactly like Whisper, headphones clamped to their ears, grinning at each other like they'd each won a bet. The same beep was pouring out of every speaker.

"You're hearing it too," said a technician, noticing Eli's stunned face but not questioning how he'd gotten there, as if strange boys turning up at history were simply part of the job tonight. "Everyone's hearing it. Ordinary radios, all over the planet."

"What is it?" Eli asked, though he already suspected.

"Sputnik," the man said, savoring the word. "Launched today — **October 4, 1957**. About **58 centimeters wide**, roughly the size of a beach ball, and right now it's the first man-made object ever to circle the Earth."

Eli stared up at a sky he couldn't actually see anything in, just stars, and tried to picture a beach ball crossing it at thousands of miles an hour, still beeping, like it wanted to be found.

"The whole thing started as a contest," the technician went on. "Us and the Soviets. Whoever gets there first, gets the firsts. This is the first."

A month later Eli stood in the same field and heard a second signal arrive — a different beep pattern, the technicians told him, from a second satellite the Soviets had launched on **November 3, 1957**, this one carrying a passenger: a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to orbit the Earth. Eli went quiet at that, thinking about a dog up there alone, and one of the technicians, reading his face, said gently that the world had taken her to heart too, with a kind of sadness Eli recognized from how people talk about pioneers.

Then Whisper's light flared again, impatient, a new pulse pattern already stuttering out of the speaker, faster this time, almost frantic.

"IT'S CALLING AGAIN!" Eli said, and grabbed for the dial before the field could fade.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Man With No Face
chapters.text:
The new beep pattern was choppier, and Eli's ears picked out something odd in it almost immediately: two tones, alternating, like a question and an answer.

"That's not one transmitter," he muttered. "That's two sides talking back."

Whisper seemed to agree. The light dragged him sideways this time, into a low concrete room full of men in white shirts, staring at a bank of instruments and arguing about radiation counts.

"You're late," one of them said to Eli, not unkindly, and shoved a clipboard his way as if he belonged there. "Explorer 1 went up **January 31, 1958**. First American satellite. And its instruments just found something nobody expected."

Eli scanned the clipboard. Counts climbing, then flatlining, then climbing again as the satellite crossed certain points in its orbit.

"A radiation belt," Eli said slowly. "Something's trapped up there. A ring of it, circling the planet."

"The **Van Allen radiation belt**," the man confirmed, delighted, like Eli had just said the answer to a riddle the whole room had been chewing on. "Charged particles, caught in Earth's magnetic field like iron filings around a horseshoe magnet. Nobody knew it was there until this little satellite flew through it."

Eli grinned. A whole invisible ring around the planet, discovered because somebody launched a can full of instruments into the sky. That was the kind of thing that made physics worth doing.

The Sputnik shock, the man explained, had moved fast. Stunned that the Soviets had gotten there first, the United States had built an entire new agency in response: **NASA**, which started operating on **October 1, 1958**. "We weren't going to let them win the whole race on the first lap," he said.

On a side table, a newsreel projector flickered through grainy Soviet footage — rockets, engineers, applause — and Eli noticed something strange. Every face in every frame was blurred or turned away, except for one man whose name was never once spoken.

"Who's that?" Eli asked, pointing.

The room went quiet in a way that told him he'd asked the right question.

"Nobody knows," the technician said. "The Soviets call him only the **Chief Designer**. He runs their whole rocket program, and they've made sure not one photo of his face has ever left the country. Whoever he is, we may never find out."

Eli looked at the blurred figure a long moment, filing the mystery away like a loose thread he intended to pull on later.

Then Whisper buzzed against his hip, hungry for a new answer, and the beep this time came fast and sharp, almost like a countdown.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Hundred and Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
A countdown. That part was easy. Any kid who'd watched a rocket launch on a screen knew what that rhythm meant.

"Something's about to go up," Eli said, and Whisper's light agreed, yanking him into a crowd standing outside under an open sky, every face tipped back, waiting.

"You made it just in time," said a woman nearby, handing him a pair of borrowed binoculars without asking where he'd come from. "**April 12, 1961**. Any minute now."

The rocket went up on a column of fire, and Eli did the mental math without meaning to — if that capsule reached orbital speed, it would circle the whole Earth once in roughly ninety minutes to two hours, depending on altitude. Close enough, as it turned out.

"Vostok 1," the woman said, watching his lips move. "Carrying Yuri Gagarin. First human being ever to leave the atmosphere. He'll orbit the Earth once, about **108 minutes**, and then he's home."

Eli let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. A hundred and eight minutes to become the first person in history to see the whole curve of the planet at once. He tried to imagine it and couldn't quite get there.

Three weeks later — the scene shifted again, the same waiting crowd but smaller, the flags different — Eli watched a second launch, shorter and stubbier, the capsule barely clearing the pad before arcing back down.

"Alan Shepard," someone told him. "**May 5, 1961**. First American in space, aboard **Freedom 7**. Didn't orbit — too short a flight for that — but he got there, and that's what mattered to everyone watching."

Eli understood instantly why the distinction mattered to a physicist even if it looked small to everyone else: reaching space and reaching orbital velocity were two completely different problems, and the Americans had just solved the easier one first.

Three weeks after that, in a packed hall with a podium and too many microphones, Eli heard a voice promise something enormous.

"On **May 25, 1961**," a man near him explained, nodding toward the podium, "President Kennedy is about to challenge the whole country to land a man on the Moon — and bring him home safe — before the decade is out."

Eli watched the speech land across the room like a dropped stone, ripples spreading outward, and understood, maybe for the first time, that a sentence could be a kind of rocket too — something launched on faith that still had to be built, piece by piece, to actually get anywhere.

Whisper buzzed again, softer this time, almost thoughtful, like it was choosing its next stop carefully.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Forty-Eight Times Around
chapters.text:
The next beep had a strange, steady lilt to it, almost musical, and Eli caught himself trying to count a rhythm in it before he realized — this one didn't need decoding. Whisper was simply humming, pleased with itself.

He landed in a crowd again, except this time half the signs people held were in a language he didn't recognize, and half the faces around him were turned toward the sky with the particular awe reserved for someone doing something nobody expected them to do.

"Vostok 6," said a woman beside him, beaming. "Launched **June 16, 1963**."

"Who's flying it?" Eli asked.

"Valentina Tereshkova," the woman said, like the answer gave her joy just to say out loud. "First woman in space. She'll orbit the Earth **48 times** before she's done."

Forty-eight times. Eli tried to picture the Earth scrolling past a capsule window again and again, sunrise after sunrise, and realized that whatever else the Space Race was about, it kept being, underneath everything, a race to prove that the sky didn't belong to any one kind of person.

"They wanted a first the Americans hadn't claimed yet," the woman added, with the dry satisfaction of someone describing a well-played chess move. "And they got one."

Eli laughed. Even up here, apparently, it was still a race, score kept in a column nobody admitted to keeping out loud.

He stayed long enough to watch the capsule's contrail fade into the blue, then felt Whisper tug at his pocket again, already restless, already counting down to wherever it wanted to go next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Ten Minutes Outside
chapters.text:
This time the beep came with a hiss underneath it, like static with a heartbeat, and Eli knew before Whisper even finished pulling him through that this one would be stranger than the rest.

He arrived floating — or at least, the people around him were floating, strapped into chairs bolted to a capsule wall, watching a small round window with their breath held.

"**March 18, 1965**," someone said beside him, voice tight with nerves and excitement both. "Voskhod 2. Alexei Leonov is outside the capsule right now."

Outside. Eli looked at the window and understood what that word meant up here: a man, tethered by a single cable, floating in the open vacuum of space with nothing between him and the entire universe but a suit.

"First spacewalk in history," the voice continued. "About **ten minutes** out there, and then back inside."

Ten minutes didn't sound like much from a bedroom floor. Floating weightless outside a tin can traveling thousands of miles an hour, it sounded like forever. Eli found himself holding his own breath until a small cheer went up around him and he understood: Leonov was back inside, safe, the hatch sealed, the whole room exhaling at once.

"Ten minutes to become the first person ever to leave a spacecraft in orbit," Eli said quietly, mostly to himself. "That's a pretty good ten minutes."

The cheering crew nearby didn't disagree.

Whisper buzzed once more, a slower, lower tone this time, almost solemn, and Eli felt the light drag him forward through years rather than weeks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Photograph Nobody Planned
chapters.text:
The solemn tone made sense the moment Eli landed, because the first thing anyone told him was a name.

"Korolev," said a man quietly, not looking up from a newspaper. "The Chief Designer. Turns out that's who he was all along — Sergei Korolev, the man who ran the whole Soviet rocket program from the shadows. He died back in **1966**, and only after that did anyone finally learn his name."

Eli thought of the blurred photograph from the newsreel, years back now in his own timeline, and felt something settle into place. A mystery with an ending after all, even if it was a quiet one.

Then the scene around him shifted — a capsule window again, except this time nobody was looking outward at a planet below. They were looking back at it.

"**December 1968**," someone told him. "Apollo 8. First crew ever to orbit the Moon."

Eli pressed close to the window glass beside a young astronaut named William Anders, who had a camera raised and was muttering under his breath about f-stops and light, and then simply stopped talking.

There it was. Earth, hanging whole and blue and achingly small above the gray curve of the Moon, half in shadow, half lit, like it had wandered into the frame by accident.

Anders took the shot without seeming to decide to. Nobody had planned the photograph; nobody had trained for it. It just happened, because a man looked up from his instruments at exactly the right second.

"That picture's going to outlive every single one of us," Eli said, and nobody in the capsule argued.

He stood there a long moment, watching the Earth turn slowly in the window, before Whisper's light began to pull again, gentler this time, as if it too understood that nothing after this view was going to look quite as small.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The next signal didn't hiss or buzz. It roared — an actual sound, mechanical and enormous, like the whole world had cleared its throat at once.

Eli landed flat on his back in grass, staring straight up at a rocket so tall it didn't seem to fit inside the sky.

"**Saturn V**," said a man lying in the grass beside him, as calm as if enormous rockets were parked in fields all the time. "**363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty. Built mostly by a team led by Wernher von Braun — he built rockets for Germany once, a long time before any of this, and ended up leading the whole Saturn V program for NASA."

Eli didn't even try to find words. He just watched it climb, trailing fire, shrinking slowly into a bright dot and then into nothing at all.

The field blurred and reformed into a cramped, dim room crowded with people leaning toward a television screen, and the date someone murmured made Eli's chest go tight: **July 20, 1969**.

On the screen, a ladder. A boot. A boot touching gray dust.

"Neil Armstrong," the room breathed, almost as one voice. "First person to walk on the Moon."

A tinny voice crackled through the television speakers, something about a small step and a giant leap, and the whole room erupted.

"HE'S ON THE MOON!" Eli shouted along with everyone else, because some things are simply too big to say quietly.

"Buzz Aldrin joined him down there a few minutes later," someone told him once the cheering settled. "And up above them both, alone the whole time, Michael Collins was flying the command module — **Columbia** — around and around the Moon, waiting to bring them home."

Eli thought about that for a while: three men on one mission, and only two of them ever got to stand on anything. Collins had circled a whole world, utterly alone, trusting the other two to make it back down safely and then back up again.

"Between **1969 and 1972**," the man added, "twelve Americans will have walked on the Moon, across six successful landings. Armstrong and Aldrin are just the first."

Twelve. Eli turned the number over like a stone in his pocket, already composing the question he'd ask Whisper next: who were the other ten, and what did each of them see up there that nobody else ever would?

But Whisper had other plans. Its light surged up around him with an urgency Eli hadn't felt before, almost alarmed, and he barely had time to brace before the room vanished.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Handshake
chapters.text:
The alarm in Whisper's light turned out to be justified. Eli landed in a room full of people hunched over consoles, faces pale, nobody cheering at all.

"**1970**," someone said, voice clipped and fast. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon."

Eli's stomach dropped — but the room, tense as it was, wasn't a room full of despair. It was a room full of people working a problem, fast and methodical, the way Eli himself worked through a stuck equation.

"The crew's alive," the man added quickly, reading Eli's face. "Crippled ship, but alive. Every engineer in this building is figuring out how to get them home using nothing but what's already on board."

Eli watched them do it — watched scraps of cardboard and tape and sheer stubborn physics turn into a fix nobody had designed in advance — and understood that this, too, was what the Space Race had always been: not just rockets and firsts, but people refusing to let a bad day become a worse one.

"They made it," the man said at last, some hours later by the room's clock, and the whole console bank finally broke into the cheer Eli had been waiting for. "Safely returned to Earth, every single one of them."

Eli let his shoulders drop for the first time in what felt like days.

The last pull from Whisper was the gentlest yet, barely a tug, and it set him down somewhere warm and quiet — two spacecraft docked together in orbit, one American, one Soviet, their crews floating through a connecting hatch to shake hands in the middle.

"**July 17, 1975**," a voice told him, soft with something like relief. "Apollo-Soyuz. After everything — Sputnik, Gagarin, the Moon, all of it — this is how the Space Race actually ends. Not with a winner. With a handshake."

Eli watched the two crews grin at each other through the open hatch, two sides of a contest that had somehow turned, in the end, into something closer to a friendship, and felt Whisper's light finally go soft and warm instead of urgent.

It set him down gently back in the garage, workbench and soldering iron exactly where he'd left them. Whisper sat dark and quiet, its dial no longer glowing, its tubes cool to the touch — except for one small thing. Tucked beside the dial, where nothing had been before, sat a scrap of yellowed paper with two words written on it in a careful, unfamiliar hand: **Chief Designer**.

Eli smiled, pocketed it, and reached for his soldering iron. There was still a lot of history left on that dial, and he intended to find all of it.

story.subtitle: A ship, a map, and a journey to the bottom of the sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Compass That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Hana lay on her bedroom floor, tweezers in hand, snapping tiny brass rails onto a half-built model ship.

Pinned above her desk was a map of the Atlantic Ocean, crossed with red string marking real shipping routes. She had drawn every line herself, tracing them off an old atlas until her wrist ached.

On her desk sat a leftover piece from the kit: a brass sextant, shaped like a small sunburst. It was supposed to be decoration. Tonight, it glowed gold.

Hana set down her tweezers. The light got brighter, and a man no taller than her thumb stepped off the dial and onto her blueprint sheet.

He wore a flat cap and overalls dusted with rust. "Name's Harland," he said, brushing off his sleeve. "Fancy a trip to Belfast? The year is **1909**."

"Belfast, Ireland?" Hana said. "That's on my map. I've got a pin right there."

"Then you already know the way," said Harland. He tapped the sunburst twice.

The bedroom walls folded away like pages in a pop-up book. Cranes and smoke and hammering took their place.

They stood on a wooden platform above a shipyard the size of a small town. Men crawled over a skeleton of steel beams — three of them, side by side.

"Three ships?" Hana asked. "Who builds three at once?"

"White Star Line does," said Harland. "Sister ships. **Olympic**, **Titanic**, and **Britannic**. Built together, here at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard in Belfast."

Hana pointed at the middle skeleton, the tallest of the three. "That one's further along than the others."

"Good eye. Her backbone — we call it the **keel**, the long beam a ship's whole body gets built on — went down on **31 March 1909**. That's Titanic. You're standing right where she was born."

Hana grinned, and somewhere below them a riveter's hammer rang out like a bell, over and over, building a ship one metal rivet at a time.

"Better get used to that sound," said Harland. "You've got a long build ahead of you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Funnels, Sixteen Rooms
chapters.text:
Two years flickered by in a blink of the compass light. Suddenly the skeleton wore skin: steel plates, four enormous funnels, portholes in neat rows.

Thousands of people lined the shipyard fence, waving flags. Something huge was about to move.

"Launch day," said Harland. "**31 May 1911**. She's ready for the water."

With a groan and a great hiss of grease, the hull began to slide. Hana held her breath as it crashed into the harbor, throwing up a wall of spray.

**SPLOOSH!**

"She's afloat!" Hana shouted, soaked from fifty feet away.

Up close, the ship looked even stranger. Hana counted the funnels, the huge smokestacks on top. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Why does the fourth one look different?"

Harland chuckled. "Sharp eyes again. Three funnels carry real smoke from the engines. The fourth one is empty. It's there to make her look bigger and grander."

"A fake funnel," said Hana. "That's cheating."

"That's shipbuilding," said Harland.

Below deck, the air buzzed with reporters and builders, all talking about one thing. Hana caught the same word floating everywhere: unsinkable.

"Why does everyone keep saying that?" she asked.

Harland led her to a cutaway model showing the ship's insides, carved up into separate sealed rooms. "**Sixteen watertight compartments**," he said. "Walls built so sturdy that if water got into one room, it could be sealed off before it spread to the next. People started calling her nearly unsinkable."

Hana studied the model, tracing the dividing walls with her finger. "Nearly," she repeated. "Not the same thing as actually."

"No," Harland agreed. "It never is."

He said it lightly. But something in his voice made Hana look up, and for a second the busy shipyard seemed quieter than before.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton and the Missing Boats
chapters.text:
Southampton docks roared with noise: horns, gulls, a brass band somewhere Hana couldn't see.

"**10 April 1912**," said Harland. "Maiden voyage. Her very first trip out, bound for New York City."

Crowds pressed the rails, waving handkerchiefs at the ship towering above them. Hana craned her neck all the way up and still couldn't see the top.

"She's enormous," Hana breathed. "How long is she really?"

"**About 882 feet**," said Harland. "**Roughly 269 meters**. The biggest ship afloat anywhere that year."

Hana walked the dock, matching her own steps to the length painted on a sign. She stopped counting her strides somewhere past sixty.

Near the gangway, she spotted something odd: a row of small wooden boats hanging from the upper deck, far fewer than she'd expect for a ship this size.

"Harland. Count those with me."

They counted together, Hana tallying on her palm the way she marked distances on her bedroom map.

"Those boats," said Harland, "could carry **about 1,178 people**."

Hana frowned. "That's not very many. Look how many people are getting on."

"You're right to notice," said Harland quietly. "There were rules back then about how many lifeboats a ship needed, based on a ship's size, not how many people she actually carried. Titanic followed every rule there was. The rules themselves just weren't enough."

Hana looked from the tiny boats up to the towering decks. "Somebody should fix that."

"Somebody will," said Harland. "Hang onto that thought."

He took her hand as the gangway horn blasted one long note, and the ship pulled slowly away from the dock, out toward open water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Night the Sea Turned Hard
chapters.text:
Four nights later, the sea had gone flat and silent, black as ink, with no moon at all.

Hana stood at the rail beside Harland, her breath turning to fog in the cold air.

"**14 April 1912**," said Harland. "Almost midnight."

Then she felt it before she heard it: a long, low shudder through the deck, like a giant fingernail scraping the hull.

"What was that?" Hana asked.

"**Around 11:40 p.m.**," said Harland, "Titanic struck an iceberg, out here in the icy North Atlantic."

Hana remembered the cutaway model back at the shipyard. The sealed rooms. Nearly unsinkable. She hadn't wanted to be right about anything.

Down in a cramped radio room, two men hunched over a machine clicking out dots and dashes. Hana recognized the pattern from her map legends: Morse code, a way of spelling words out in short and long taps.

"That's **wireless**," said Harland. "A way to send messages through the air, no wires needed. Operators **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** are calling for help."

"What are they sending?"

"First the old distress call, **CQD**. Then something newer. Three short, three long, three short."

Hana worked it out herself, counting the taps on her fingers. "**SOS**," she said.

"Brand new that year," said Harland. "Nobody was sure it would catch on. Tonight, it did."

Out across the black water, another ship picked up the signal and turned, engines straining, toward Titanic's position.

"Someone's coming," said Harland.

Hana exhaled, fog curling from her mouth. "Good," she said. "Then let's go find the boats."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Boats on Black Water
chapters.text:
The deck tilted, just slightly, enough that Hana had to plant her feet to stay steady.

Crew members helped passengers down into the small boats, lowering them toward the water one careful creak at a time.

Near the bridge, a man in a captain's coat stood calm and still, giving orders without ever raising his voice.

"**Captain Edward John Smith**," said Harland. "One of White Star's most experienced commanders. He's staying aboard."

Hana didn't ask why. Somehow, she understood.

From somewhere on deck, music drifted through the cold air — violin and cello, steady and clear.

"Is that a band?" Hana asked.

"Led by **Wallace Hartley**," said Harland. "People say the band kept playing right to the end, to keep everyone calm. That part might be stretched a little in the retelling — nobody wrote down a perfect set list — but passengers really did hear music that night."

Near one of the boats, a woman wrapped a fur coat tighter and took up an oar without being asked, rowing like she'd done it her whole life.

"Who's that?" Hana asked.

"**Margaret Brown**," said Harland. "Everyone just calls her Molly. After tonight, people will call her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'"

Hana smiled. "There's that word again."

"Fits her better than it fit the ship," said Harland.

A small bark caught Hana's ear. Two fluffy little **Pomeranian** dogs rode tucked inside coats in one of the boats, carried along by their owners.

"Even the dogs made it," Hana said, delighted.

"Some did," said Harland. "Small boats, but kind hands."

The little boats pulled away from the ship, spreading out across the dark water, waiting for morning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Carpathia at Dawn
chapters.text:
Dawn came up gray and freezing, and with it, lights on the horizon.

"**Carpathia**," said Harland. "She raced through the whole night to reach you."

One by one, the little lifeboats rowed toward the steamship, and passengers climbed rope ladders up her side, wrapped in blankets handed down from the deck.

Hana counted the boats coming in, the same way she'd counted them hanging empty back at the dock in Southampton.

Not everyone made it into one.

"**More than 1,500 people** didn't get to come home," said Harland quietly. "There just weren't enough boats, and not enough time."

Hana was quiet for a moment, watching the gray water.

"But people were saved," she said. "Carpathia got here."

"She did," said Harland. "Everyone in those lifeboats made it. And afterward, people made sure next time there would be boats enough for everyone, no matter the ship."

"What did they change?"

"Two big things," said Harland. "First, a group called the **International Ice Patrol** started watching the North Atlantic for icebergs, so ships would know where the danger was."

Hana's eyes lit up. "Like — marking them on a map?"

"Exactly like that," said Harland. "Someone has to draw the warning before anyone else can read it."

"And the second thing?"

"A new rulebook for ships everywhere, called **SOLAS** — Safety of Life at Sea. From then on, every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard, not just what the old rules required."

Hana looked back at the lifeboats, safely emptied now, swinging against Carpathia's side.

"Good," she said. "That's the fix."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Twelve Thousand Feet Down
chapters.text:
The compass flared, and the gray morning dissolved into darkness again, deeper and colder than any night before.

"Where are we now?" Hana asked.

"**1 September 1985**," said Harland. "Seventy-three years later. We're not above the water this time. We're under it."

Through a small round window, Hana watched a searchlight sweep across an empty, silent seafloor, soft mud and stillness stretching in every direction.

"**About 12,500 feet down**," said Harland. "Nearly 3,800 meters. An explorer named **Robert Ballard** led the team looking for her."

Hana pressed close to the window, watching shapes drift past in the gloom: a boiler, a railing, a single shoe resting in the mud.

Then something huge took shape out of the dark — a wall of rusted steel, enormous, unmistakable.

"There," Hana said, pointing. "That's her, isn't it?"

"That's her," said Harland.

"**WE FOUND HER!**" Hana shouted, and her voice rang off the little window.

She studied the wreck's shape, something not quite matching the ship she'd watched slide into the water back in Belfast.

"She's in two pieces," Hana said slowly. "Why is she split?"

"Good catch," said Harland. "Ballard's team found her broken into two main sections, sitting a distance apart on the seafloor, around **370 miles off Newfoundland, Canada**."

Hana traced the distance in her head, the way she traced routes on her bedroom map, picturing Newfoundland's coastline out past the dark water above them.

"I'd put a pin right there," she said.

"Then you already know more than most mapmakers," said Harland.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Ship-Shaped Museum
chapters.text:
The dark seafloor melted away, replaced by daylight and a building shaped like a ship's pointed front, all glass and silver, rising above a harbor.

"Belfast again," said Harland. "**2012** this time. A hundred years on."

"**Titanic Belfast**," Hana read off a sign near the entrance. "This is where we started."

Inside, glass cases held objects pulled up from the seafloor: dinner plates, buttons, a single leather shoe, cleaned and carefully lit.

"All real," said Harland. "Raised from the wreck, kept safe in museums all over the world now, so people don't forget."

Hana leaned close to a case holding a small brass sextant, nearly identical to the one on her own desk at home.

"People still want to hear this story," she said.

"Plenty have told it," said Harland. "There's even a very famous movie about her, made back in **1997**. Became one of the biggest films ever made."

"I've seen it," said Hana. "Well — parts of it."

Harland raised an eyebrow, somehow, despite being made of brass. "Bedtime's bedtime," he said. "Even for movies."

Hana laughed. The compass on the sextant model began to glow again, gentler this time, pulling them both back.

The museum faded. The harbor faded. And Hana was on her bedroom carpet again, tweezers still in hand, her half-built model ship finished at last, every brass rail in place.

On her wall, a new pin sat in her map, right off the coast of Newfoundland, string running back to a little dot marked Belfast.

Harland, tiny again, tipped his cap from the edge of the sunburst compass. "Until the next crossing," he said, and the gold light dimmed to nothing.

Hana set the finished ship on her windowsill, where it could catch the morning light.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a new pin to put on the map.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Time Machine
story.subtitle: A blocky guide takes Ben on a tour through video game history.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Dot in the Lab
chapters.text:
Ben sat on his bedroom floor, drawing a pixel dog on his tablet. Each square was its own color. He loved counting every tiny block until the dog looked just right.

Then the screen flickered. Green. Black. Green again.

"Whoa," Ben said. "Did you just glitch?"

A burst of tiny squares popped out of the screen. They swirled together into a blocky little creature with blinking eyes, like a sprite that had escaped the game.

"BOOP!" it said. "I'm Blip. I live inside old screens. Want to see where games began?"

Before Ben could answer, green light filled the room. WHOOSH. The floor turned into a glowing grid, and his chair became a lab stool.

They landed in a big room full of humming machines. A scientist leaned over a strange box with a round screen.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Blip said. "It's a machine that draws wiggly lines of light to test electricity."

The scientist, **William Higinbotham**, flipped a switch. A green dot bounced across the round screen, back and forth.

Ben leaned closer. "It's a ball! Is that tennis?"

"Good eye," said Blip. "In **1958**, at a lab called **Brookhaven**, he built this. He called it Tennis for Two. It's one of the very first video games ever made."

Ben swung an imaginary paddle at the dot. People lined up to try it, laughing every time they missed.

"This is way before Minecraft," Ben said.

"Everything starts somewhere," Blip said. "Ready for stop two?"

"BOOP! Let's go," Ben grinned.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Humming Computer Room
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. They landed in a room the size of a garage, filled with one giant machine.

"That's a computer?" Ben asked. "It's huge!"

"This one's called a **PDP-1**," Blip said. "Back then, computers filled whole rooms."

A student typed quickly at a keyboard. Two little triangle ships appeared on the round screen, shooting tiny dots at each other.

"In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends made this," Blip said. "They called it Spacewar! It was one of the first computer games made just for fun."

Ben studied the ships. "They look like pixel art. Like, really early pixel art."

"That's exactly what they are," Blip said.

Ben watched the dots fly past the ships, missing every time. "What if the ships could spin around? Then you could dodge better."

The student typed something new. The ship spun in a slow circle.

"Whoa, it worked!" Ben said.

"Players kept asking for new tricks," Blip said. "That's how games grow. Somebody always asks, what if?"

Ben counted how many shots missed before one finally hit. "Eleven misses. That guy needs practice."

Blip laughed, a sound like a tiny beep. "Next stop is a house with a brand-new kind of television."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: A Box for the TV
chapters.text:
They landed in a cozy living room. A man sat on the floor surrounded by wires and plastic parts.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Blip said. "People later called him the father of video games."

Ben watched him connect wires to an old television. "What's he building?"

"A **prototype**," Blip said. "That means a first try, before the real thing gets made. He called it the Brown Box."

Ralph flipped a switch. Two white paddles appeared on the TV screen, with a square dot bouncing between them.

"It's like Tennis for Two," Ben said, "but on a TV, in someone's living room."

"Exactly," Blip said. "In **1972**, his invention became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game console you could play at home."

Ben pointed at the screen. "What if you stuck colored plastic over it? Like, orange for a basketball court?"

Blip nodded. "People really did stick plastic sheets right over their screens, just like that, to make it look fancier."

The room suddenly shifted into a noisy arcade, machines blinking everywhere. A new game sat in the middle: two paddles, one ball, simple white lines.

"That same year," Blip said, "**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called Atari. They made an arcade game called **Pong**."

A crowd of kids lined up with coins in their hands.

"Some people say one Pong machine got so stuffed with coins it actually jammed shut," Blip said. "That part might be stretched a little tall, but it shows how fast everyone fell in love with it."

Ben laughed. "A coin traffic jam."

"BOOP! Let's see what came after paddles," Blip said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Swap the Cartridge
chapters.text:
They landed in a den with a big wood-paneled TV. A kid was sliding a flat plastic rectangle into a slot.

"That's a **cartridge**," Blip said. "It's like a little plastic box with a game stored inside. You could swap it out for a different one."

Ben's eyes lit up. "Like changing worlds in Minecraft! You don't need a whole new game machine, you just pick a new game."

"Right," Blip said. "In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players do exactly that."

The screen flashed, and rows of blocky aliens marched sideways, slowly dropping lower.

"Whoa, who made this one?" Ben asked.

"A designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**," Blip said. "In **1978**, he made **Space Invaders** for a company called Taito. It caused a giant craze in arcades everywhere."

Ben counted the aliens. "Five rows. Eleven across. I'd shoot the edges first, so they can't speed up as fast."

He pretended to fire. Two rows of aliens blinked out.

"Good strategy," Blip said. "Players lined up around the block to try that game."

"It's basically pixel art that shoots lasers," Ben said.

"That's one way to put it," Blip laughed. "Next stop, a hungry yellow circle."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hungry Circle and the Buried Games
chapters.text:
A bright maze appeared, glowing blue. A yellow circle zipped through it, gobbling up little dots.

"This is **Pac-Man**," Blip said. "A designer named **Toru Iwatani** made it in **1980** for a company called Namco."

Ben watched the circle chase four colorful ghosts, then turn and chase them back after eating a bigger dot.

"Why's he shaped like that?" Ben asked.

"People say he got the idea from looking at a pizza with one slice missing," Blip said. "Nobody's totally sure that story's true, but it's a fun one."

Ben laughed. "Pac-Man is a pizza. I'm never looking at pizza the same way again."

The scene shifted. Shelves of game cartridges crowded a store, dusty and unwanted.

"By **1983**, so many rushed, sloppy games got made that shoppers stopped trusting them," Blip said. "Stores had way too many games and not enough buyers. People call it the video game crash."

Ben frowned. "That sounds sad."

"It wasn't the end, though," Blip said. "Watch this."

A truck rolled up to a big dirt pit in the desert and dumped boxes of cartridges inside.

"Some unsold games, including one called E.T., got buried in a landfill in New Mexico," Blip said. "A landfill is just a huge dump where trash gets buried."

"Did anyone ever check if that's true?" Ben asked.

"Good question," Blip said. "In **2014**, diggers actually dug there and found the buried cartridges, just like the story said."

"So it's buried treasure," Ben said, "treasure nobody wanted."

Blip giggled. "Something like that. Don't worry, Ben, games were about to make the biggest comeback ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
They landed in a toy store. A new gray box sat on a shelf, with a game box beside it.

"In **1985**, Nintendo brought games back to America with this," Blip said. "It's called the **NES**. It came packed with a brand new game."

The TV flicked on. A small mustached man in overalls jumped over a mushroom creature.

"That's **Mario**!" Ben shouted.

"A designer named **Shigeru Miyamoto** made **Super Mario Bros.** that same year," Blip said. "Mario became the most famous game character of all time."

Ben watched Mario leap onto a floating block. "What if he jumped on top instead of running into it?"

On screen, Mario did exactly that, bopping the block from below. A coin popped out.

"You've got good instincts," Blip said.

The scene shifted to a snowy office in another country, where a scientist stared at a screen full of falling shapes.

"This is **Alexey Pajitnov**," Blip said. "In **1984**, in Moscow, he invented a puzzle game called **Tetris**. Blocks fall, and you fit them together."

Ben watched a long piece drop into a gap, clearing a whole row with a satisfying CLACK.

"It's like stacking blocks in Minecraft," Ben said, "except they disappear when you get it right."

"Exactly like that," Blip said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Speedy Hedgehogs and Spinning Discs
chapters.text:
The room spun into a blur of colors. Blip grabbed Ben's sleeve. "Hang on, this part moves fast."

A blue hedgehog blasted across the screen, curling into a spinning ball.

"In **1991**, a company called Sega made **Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "He was built to be fast, to race against Mario."

"He's basically a speedrunner," Ben said.

Next, a silver disc spun inside a new gray console.

"In **1994**, **Sony** made the **PlayStation**," Blip said. "It used **CDs**, shiny discs, instead of cartridges. That meant games could have longer stories and fuller sound."

The scene flicked again. Two kids sat at computers connected by a tangle of cables, grinning at their screens.

"In **1993**, a game called **Doom** let players team up or compete through a bunch of connected computers," Blip said. "Friends plugging their computers together to play got called a LAN party."

"Like a sleepover, but for games," Ben said.

"Exactly," Blip said.

One more flash, and a family stood in a living room swinging their arms at a TV, holding small white controllers.

"In **2006**, Nintendo's **Wii** let you swing the controller like a tennis racket or a sword," Blip said. "Even people who never played games before started trying it."

Ben swung an imaginary controller. "This is a lot of history for one afternoon."

"We're nearly caught up to you," Blip said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Blocks
chapters.text:
The light shifted to soft blue, and Ben recognized the shape of a block-built world stretching in every direction.

"Wait," Ben said. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," Blip said. "A developer named **Markus Persson**, who people called **Notch**, released it in **2011**."

Ben looked around at the cube-shaped trees and grassy hills. "This is literally the thing I play every day."

"It became the best-selling video game ever made," Blip said.

Ben grinned, thinking about every tower, every farm, every pixel-art banner he'd ever built. "I guess I'm part of this story too."

"You always were," Blip said.

One last WHOOSH carried them into a bright museum hallway, glass cases glowing with old consoles and posters.

"This is **The Strong museum**, in Rochester, New York," Blip said. "In **2015**, it opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**, to remember games that mattered."

Ben peered into a case holding an old Pong machine, a Mario cartridge, a dusty Tetris disk.

"They're like fossils," Ben said, then paused. "Wait, not fossils. Like, old treasures."

"Good save," Blip laughed.

Then the museum lights blurred into green and black, and the floor turned back to carpet.

Ben blinked. He was back in his room, tablet glowing in his lap. His pixel dog drawing was still there, finished, every square exactly where he'd left it.

Sitting beside the tablet was one tiny square pixel, glowing faintly green, shaped like the dot from Tennis for Two.

"Blip?" Ben whispered.

No answer. Just the little glowing pixel, and a quiet room.

Ben tucked it under his pillow and climbed into bed, smiling at the ceiling.
