story.title: Theo and the Secret History of Video Games
story.subtitle: One glowing screen, a thousand old games, and one bedtime deadline.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Dot That Wouldn't Quit
chapters.text:
Theo was deep into building a new obstacle course in Roblox Studio, snapping blocks together the way other kids snap together LEGO bricks. His soccer ball sat forgotten by the door, laces still muddy from practice.

Then his monitor hiccupped. The screen flashed black, then a crawling green line, like something off an old hospital monitor, bounced across it.

A tiny dot of light rose off the glass and hovered by his ear. "Finally," it said. "Do you know how long I've been waiting for someone who actually likes building games?"

Theo jumped back so fast his chair nearly tipped. "Who — what are you?"

"Call me Blip," said the dot, flickering between green and white. "I live in screens. Any screen. Yours just happened to be on."

Before Theo could ask a follow-up question, the green line on his monitor arranged itself into two paddles and a bouncing dot — exactly like the simplest game he'd ever coded.

"Recognize it?" Blip asked.

Theo squinted. "It's basically Pong. But... old."

"Older than Pong," Blip said. "This is **Tennis for Two**, built in **1958** by a scientist named **William Higinbotham**. He drew it on an **oscilloscope** — that's a screen scientists used to watch wavy lines of electricity — at a science lab called **Brookhaven National Laboratory**. Nobody was trying to invent a video game. He just wanted his lab's open house to be less boring."

"So it worked," Theo said, grinning, and grabbed the two knobs that had appeared on his desk like controller sticks.

The dot bounced. Theo twisted a knob at the last second and sent it arcing back over the invisible net. The screen chimed, an old-timey arcade chime, and the green world around him folded inward like a closing laptop lid.

"Nicely returned," Blip said. "Ready to see where that bounce led?"

"Lead the way," said Theo. "I've got nothing but bedtime."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Fridge-Sized Computer
chapters.text:
The green world dissolved into a hum of machinery. Theo stood in a room filled with blinking cabinets the size of refrigerators, wires taped along the floor like field markings.

"This," Blip said, perching on a reel of tape, "is a **PDP-1**. One of the first computers anybody could actually play with, instead of just use for serious work."

A knot of college students crowded around a round screen, arguing about controls. One handed Theo a box bristling with switches.

"That's not a controller," Theo said. "That's a math test."

"Figure it out," Blip said. "You build games. You can read a control scheme."

Theo flipped switches, testing one at a time, the way he'd test spawn points in Roblox Studio. A triangle ship jerked left. Another switch spun it. On the third try he found the thrust switch, and the ship shot forward across the round screen, dodging another student's ship.

"There," Theo said. "Twin ships, shooting at each other. It's basically a 1v1 match from a thousand years ago."

"Sixty-some years ago," Blip corrected. "This is **Spacewar!**, made in **1962** by an MIT student named **Steve Russell** and his friends. People came from all over campus just to take a turn."

One of the students whooped as Theo's ship clipped theirs and sent it spinning. "Not bad for switches," the student said.

Theo grinned, pocketing an invisible win. "Soccer rule," he said. "Footwork first, fancy stuff later."

Blip spun in a tight little circle, which for a dot of light meant something like a laugh. "Speaking of footwork — someone's about to invent the first TV you can actually play on."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box in the Attic and the Jammed Machine
chapters.text:
The hum of the lab faded into a quiet living room with shag carpet and a TV the size of a washing machine.

A man with a soldering iron was hunched over a plain brown box, wires spilling out the back, wired straight into the television. "Just need the dot to move right," he muttered.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Blip said. "People later called him **the father of video games**. In the late 1960s, he built this prototype, nicknamed the **Brown Box** — the first real idea for playing a game on your own television."

Theo crouched beside him. On the screen, two glowing rectangles batted a square back and forth. "It's a paddle game," Theo said. "Like Tennis for Two, but on a TV instead of a lab screen."

"Exactly," said Baer, not looking up. "Give it a few years and everyone will have one of these."

He wasn't wrong. Blip tapped the air and the scene jumped to 1972: the Brown Box, shiny and boxed up now, became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first video game console anyone could buy for their own living room.

The scene jumped again, to a noisy arcade lit in red and gold, where a cabinet named **Pong** had a line of kids waiting with coins in their fists.

"Same year," Blip said. "Two guys named **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and put out their own paddle game, this one for arcades."

Theo fed a quarter into the slot and the machine made a long, grinding sound before falling silent.

"Jammed," Blip said, delighted. "Story goes an early Pong machine actually jammed solid once — stuffed completely full of quarters, because so many people wanted to play. Might be a bit of a stretch, but it tells you how fast this thing caught on."

Theo laughed, rattling the coin slot. "Guess I broke history."

"You broke a very old arcade cabinet," Blip said. "Try not to make a habit of it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Swap the Cartridge, Dodge the Aliens
chapters.text:
Next stop: a bedroom wallpapered in posters, a wood-paneled console sitting under the TV like a trophy.

"**Atari 2600**," Blip announced. "Launched in **1977**. Before this, consoles had one game built in forever. This one let you swap in plastic **cartridges** — like little save files you could plug in — so one box could play dozens of games."

Theo pulled a cartridge from a shoebox and slotted it home. "So it's like switching Roblox experiences," he said. "Same console, totally different game."

"Exactly that idea," Blip said. "People just hadn't thought of it yet."

The TV flared, and suddenly Theo wasn't just watching — he was standing inside a scrolling arcade screen, rows of blocky aliens marching down toward him.

"**Space Invaders**," Blip said, raising her voice over a rising electronic heartbeat. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** for a company called Taito. It kicked off an arcade craze across the whole world."

The aliens dropped a row, faster now. Theo's thumb found the fire button without thinking — same reflex as cutting off a breakaway on the soccer field, read the angle, move early.

He cleared the bottom row just as it reached the edge of the screen.

"Nice save," Blip said.

"That's the thing about goalkeeping," Theo said, breathing hard. "You can't wait till the ball's already past you."

Above them, the alien formation reset, ready to march again, same as it always had for kids in arcades since 1978.

"They never stop coming, by the way," Blip added. "That's the whole game."

"Cool," Theo said. "Let's not stay for round two."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Pizza With One Slice Missing
chapters.text:
The arcade glow shifted to yellow. A small round character with a hungry mouth chomped across a maze of dots, chased by four ghosts.

"**Pac-Man**," Theo said immediately. "Everyone knows Pac-Man."

"Everyone knows the character," Blip said. "Made in **1980** by a designer named **Toru Iwatani**, for a company called Namco. He's said to have gotten the idea from a pizza with one slice missing — which, if true, is the best reason anyone has ever had to invent a video game."

Theo grabbed the floating joystick and steered the yellow circle around a corner, narrowly dodging a ghost. "So he just looked at dinner and thought, character?"

"That's the story," Blip said. "Can't prove it. But it's stuck for over forty years, so somebody did something right."

Theo gobbled a row of dots, turned a corner too sharp, and nearly ran into a ghost — then spotted the flashing power dot in the corner and changed direction at the last second, scooping it up. The ghosts turned blue and fled.

"Nice read," Blip said.

"Positioning," Theo said. "Same as marking a run before the pass even happens."

The maze cleared, dots gone, ghosts retreating to their little box in the middle.

"Level one," Blip said. "Want to guess what's coming next?"

"Please don't say it's harder," Theo said.

"It's harder," Blip said. "But first — a slightly bumpy year."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Crash and the Buried Box
chapters.text:
The bright maze colors drained to gray. Shelves and shelves of game cartridges sat untouched in a store, dust thick on their boxes.

"**1983**," Blip said. "Companies rushed out so many sloppy games that people stopped trusting the shelf. Nobody knew which cartridge was actually good anymore, so a lot of people just stopped buying. The whole video game market in North America shrank hard, almost overnight."

Theo picked up a cartridge, blew dust off the label. "That's kind of sad," he said. "Like if every Roblox game suddenly got bad ratings at once."

"Pretty much," Blip said. "But here's the fun part."

The store dissolved into a moonlit stretch of New Mexico desert, a backhoe parked beside a huge hole.

"A famous story says that truckloads of unsold game cartridges — including a rushed game based on the movie E.T. — got buried right here, in a landfill," Blip said. "People told that story for thirty years, and some folks thought it was made up."

"Was it?"

"Diggers actually found the cartridges in **2014**," Blip said. "Right where the story said they'd be."

Theo grinned, kicking at the dirt with his sneaker. "So it's true true."

"True true," Blip agreed. "Business had a rough couple of years after that. Good news — somebody was about to fix it, with a plumber."

"A plumber," Theo repeated flatly.

"Trust me," Blip said, and the desert folded away like a closing browser tab.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
Theo landed in a toy-store aisle in 1985, stacked floor to ceiling with gray rectangular boxes.

"**Nintendo** brought this out to save the whole market," Blip said. "The **NES**. It came bundled with a game that made everyone care about home consoles again."

The box in Theo's hands lit up, and suddenly he was running through a pixel world of green pipes and brick blocks, a mustached plumber under his control.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," Blip said. "Designed in **1985** by **Shigeru Miyamoto**. That plumber is still gaming's most famous character, and this is where he started."

Theo jumped, stomped a mushroom creature, and punched a block overhead — gold coins spilled out, the same satisfying chime he'd heard in a hundred games since.

"Building blocks you can actually hit," Theo said. "No wonder people kept playing."

Blip swept a hand and the pipes rearranged into falling colored blocks, stacking down a narrow well.

"Different year, different country," Blip said. "**1984**, a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov** made this one, in a computer center in Moscow. Falling shapes you rotate and slot together."

"**Tetris**," Theo said, already rotating a piece in his mind, snapping an L-block into a gap like finishing a build in Roblox Studio one block at a time. The row lit up and vanished.

"Two totally different games," Theo said. "Same year, basically."

"Give or take," Blip said. "Both still being played today. Not bad for a plumber and some falling blocks from Moscow."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blue Blur, Shiny Discs, and a Roomful of Cables
chapters.text:
The brick blocks blurred into streaks of blue. Something fast shot past Theo's head, looped the level, and skidded to a stop in a shower of sparkly rings.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "Released in **1991** by Sega, a fast blue mascot — basically a company's walking logo — built specifically to give Mario some competition."

"He's fast," Theo said, impressed, as the hedgehog zipped off again.

"Speaking of fast," Blip said, and the scene flickered into a dim room full of monitors, a shiny silver disc spinning in one machine, "Sony joined the console business in **1994**, with the **PlayStation**. Games started shipping on CDs instead of cartridges, which meant room for fuller video and sound."

The nearest monitor flared into a dark corridor, two players moving through it, firing at targets, laughing over headsets.

"**1993**," Blip said. "A shooter called **Doom** got people doing something new: playing against each other, not just the computer. Friends dragged their whole computers over to one house and plugged them together with cables — a **LAN party** — just to play the same match in the same room."

Theo laughed. "That's basically a sleepover, but for gaming."

"Exactly that," Blip said. "Long before anyone had Roblox servers to jump into from their own bedroom, people needed an actual room, and actual cables, to play together."

Theo glanced at the tangle of cords behind his own desk. "Some things don't change."

"Some things get a lot easier," Blip said. "Next stop, you don't even need a controller."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Shake It, Build It
chapters.text:
Theo's hands closed around something that wasn't a joystick at all — a white remote, light as a TV clicker.

"**2006**," Blip said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. Instead of pressing buttons, you move the controller itself, and the game reads the motion."

Theo swung his arm like he was taking a free kick, and on the screen a tiny tennis racket swung to match. "It's reading me," he said, swinging again, grinning at how closely it mirrored his own motion.

"A lot of people who'd never touched a console before picked this one up," Blip said. "Grandparents. Parents. People who thought video games weren't for them."

The white remote dissolved into a familiar texture — blocky, green, square — and Theo's stomach did a small flip of recognition.

"Wait," he said. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," Blip confirmed. "Made by a Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — everyone called him **Notch** — and released in **2011**."

Theo reached out and placed a block, the simple satisfying thunk of it slotting into the world exactly like his Roblox builds back home. "It became the best-selling video game ever made," Blip went on. "One guy, one idea, blocks all the way down."

"That's basically what I do every afternoon," Theo said, placing another block just to feel it click.

"That's exactly what you do every afternoon," Blip said. "You're standing in the family tree, Theo. Hope you can see the resemblance."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back to the Green Screen
chapters.text:
One last flicker, and Theo stood in a quiet museum hall, glass cases lining the walls, a gold plaque glowing above a wall of names.

"**The Strong museum**, in **Rochester, New York**," Blip said. "They opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** here in **2015** — a wall for the games that changed everything you've played tonight."

Theo scanned the plaques: a green dot, two paddles, a yellow circle, a plumber, a falling block, a blue hedgehog, a green cube. Every stop on his own night, lined up behind glass.

"We just walked through all of it," Theo said. "Like, actually walked through it."

"Every bit of it really happened," Blip said. "Different decade, different country, different people in a lab or a bedroom somewhere — all of them just trying to make something fun."

The plaque wall dimmed, and the familiar hum of Theo's own monitor rose up around him. The green scanline bounced once more, then steadied into his half-finished Roblox build, blocks exactly where he'd left them.

Blip hovered by the screen's edge, dimmer now, more pixel than voice. "Same deal as always," she said. "I go quiet till the next screen lights up."

"You're leaving?"

"I'm waiting," Blip said. "Big difference. Go build something worth remembering."

The screen settled to its ordinary glow. Theo looked at his half-built obstacle course with new eyes — one more small level in a very long history of people just trying to make something fun.

He saved his file. By the door, his soccer ball sat exactly where he'd left it, waiting for morning.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a build to finish — and a practice before that.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbly Brick
story.subtitle: A warm, glowing tour through Earth's fiery mountains

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rumbly Brick
chapters.text:
Juno stomped her toy dinosaurs across the carpet. Stomp, stomp, STOMP!

Milo was building a tall LEGO tower beside her.

Theo sat close by. He was playing a volcano level on his tablet.

Suddenly, one of Milo's bricks began to glow. It glowed bright orange, like a tiny sunset.

Then it rumbled. RUMBLE RUMBLE RUMBLE!

"Whoa," said Milo. "My brick never did that before."

A tiny orange rock popped out of the brick. It had two round eyes and a big smile.

"Hello!" said the rock. "My name is Blaze. I am made of warm, wiggly rock. Just like a real volcano!"

Juno giggled. "You're funny."

"Want to see a real volcano?" asked Blaze. "A volcano is a hole in the ground. Hot stuff comes up from way down deep."

Theo leaned in close. "Hot stuff like what?"

"Melted rock," said Blaze. "Down under the ground, we call it magma. That's a fancy word for melted rock. When it comes up to the top, we call it lava instead."

Milo tapped the glowing brick. CLICK!

It popped open like a tiny door. Warm orange light poured out.

"Let's go see!" said Milo.

One by one, they stepped through the glowing door. WHOOSH! The living room disappeared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Giant Horseshoe
chapters.text:
They landed on a floating map, big as a swimming pool. Little red dots glowed all around one ocean.

Theo looked closer. The dots made one huge horseshoe shape. It looked like a bent goal post. He loved shapes like this, from his maps game.

"That shape has a name," said Blaze. "We call it the Ring of Fire. It goes all around one big ocean."

"Why so many volcanoes there?" asked Theo.

"The ground isn't one solid piece," said Blaze. "It's broken into giant pieces. Like puzzle pieces. We call them plates. Where two plates bump, pull apart, or slide past each other, volcanoes like to pop up."

Milo pictured his LEGO baseplates sliding apart. "Like when my baseplates don't line up!"

"Exactly," said Blaze, patting Milo's shoulder.

"How many volcanoes are on this horseshoe?" asked Theo.

"About seventy-five out of every hundred awake volcanoes on Earth," said Blaze. "They all live right along here."

Theo grinned. He pointed along the glowing line. "Let's follow it!"

They walked along the bright red path. The horseshoe curved ahead of them, waiting to be explored.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: So Many Volcanoes
chapters.text:
The path led them to a string of tall green mountains. Each one puffed a little cloud of smoke.

PUFF. PUFF. PUFF.

Juno started counting the puffs on her fingers. "One, two, three... so many!"

"You're standing in Indonesia," said Blaze. "This country has more awake volcanoes than any other place on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" asked Milo.

"Anywhere," said Blaze.

Juno kept counting, hopping from foot to foot. "Four, five, six!"

"You'd need all your fingers and toes," laughed Blaze. "And some of ours too!"

The ground felt warm under their shoes. It tickled Juno's toes, and she wiggled them happily.

Theo peeked over the edge of one mountain. A thin curl of smoke rose up. "Looks like steam from a hot dog cart," he said, and laughed at his own joke.

Juno pointed to the biggest, puffiest mountain of them all. "Let's visit that one!"

Nobody argued. Juno had picked. So Juno led the way, marching straight toward it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
Juno's puffy mountain turned out to be far across the sea, on an island called Hawaii. Warm orange rivers glowed and crept across black rock.

Milo studied the mountain's shape. It wasn't tall and pointy. It was wide and round. Like a shield. Or like one of his flattest LEGO baseplates.

"We call that a shield volcano," said Blaze. "Wide, with gentle sides. The lava here is runny, so it spreads out flat."

"Why is there a volcano all the way out here?" asked Theo. "This isn't on your horseshoe."

"Good eye," said Blaze. "Some volcanoes sit over a hotspot instead. That's a patch of extra-hot rock, way down deep. Like a little oven under the ground. Hawaii sits right on top of one."

"This one is called Kilauea," said Blaze. "It has been erupting almost all the time, for decades. Decades means lots of groups of ten years, stuck together."

Milo watched the slow orange river glow and ripple. "It's not scary. It's kind of... cozy."

"Lots of people think so too," said Blaze.

Juno reached a hand toward the warm glow. Blaze gently stopped her. "We only watch," said Blaze. "We never touch."

Juno nodded, and watched instead, eyes wide and happy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Biggest Mountain of All
chapters.text:
Next to Kilauea stood an even bigger mountain. Round and wide, like a sleeping giant.

"That one is Mauna Loa," said Blaze. "It's the biggest awake volcano on Earth. If you count all the rock inside it."

"How tall is it?" asked Theo.

"Over four thousand meters," said Blaze. "Measuring up from the sea."

Theo whistled. "That's like an entire game map, stacked straight up."

Milo giggled. "Can we build it out of LEGO when we get home?"

"You'd need a lot of bricks," said Blaze, smiling.

Juno tilted her head all the way back. She nearly tipped over looking up at the top.

Milo caught her hand just in time. "Careful," he said kindly.

"Thanks," said Juno.

They all looked up together, at the giant, gentle mountain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Brand New Island
chapters.text:
The warm wind turned into a cold sea breeze. Bubbles popped on the ocean ahead of them.

Milo spotted something rising out of the water. Dark and pointy. "Is that a shark fin?" he asked, eyes wide.

"Even better," said Blaze. "That's brand new land, being born right now."

Steam hissed as black rock pushed up out of the waves.

"In 1963, a volcano under the sea kept erupting," said Blaze. "It erupted for a long, long time. Then a whole new island popped up out of the water. They named it Surtsey."

"A volcano made an island?" asked Theo.

"This whole country, Iceland, is full of volcanoes," said Blaze. "It sits right where two giant plates are pulling apart from each other."

Juno clapped her hands. "The ground is making new land!"

"It sure is," said Blaze.

They watched from a safe, dry hill. The new island kept growing, bit by bit, out in the sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Biggest Volcano in Space
chapters.text:
CLICK! The scenery changed again. Red dust crunched under their shoes.

"Where are we now?" asked Juno.

"Mars," said Blaze. "Look up."

A mountain stretched up and up. Its top disappeared into a hazy pink sky.

Theo's mouth dropped open. "That's the biggest thing I have ever seen."

"It's called Olympus Mons," said Blaze. "The biggest volcano we know of, anywhere in space. About thirteen and a half miles tall."

"Thirteen miles tall?" said Theo. "That's enormous."

Milo tried to imagine stacking LEGO towers that high. He gave up counting.

Juno stared up, holding her dinosaur toy tight. "Even a dinosaur couldn't climb that," she whispered.

"Not even a dinosaur," agreed Blaze, chuckling.

Theo snapped a pretend screenshot with his hands, just like in his games. "I'm building this when we get home."

Blaze laughed. "Good luck finding enough blocks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
The ground changed again, to steam and bubbling pools of water.

"This is Yellowstone," said Blaze. "Underneath, there's a giant sleepy volcano. We call that kind a supervolcano, because it's extra, extra big."

Juno gasped. "Is it going to wake up?"

"Its last big eruption was about six hundred forty thousand years ago," said Blaze. "That's a very, very long time ago. Scientists don't see any sign it's waking up soon."

Milo breathed out. "Phew."

Theo spotted little machines poking out of the ground, with blinking lights. "What are those?"

"Seismographs," said Blaze. "Machines that feel tiny shakes in the ground. Even ones we can't feel with our feet. Scientists also use satellites, up in the sky, to see if the ground is puffing up. Both help them watch for signs."

Juno knelt down and poked the dark, crumbly dirt. "This dirt feels soft."

"Volcano ash turns into some of the best dirt for growing plants," said Blaze. "That's why farmers like living near volcanoes, even with the rumbling."

Theo nodded slowly. "Worth it, for dirt that good."

Blaze clapped its tiny rock hands. "Time to go home, explorers."

The glowing brick door appeared again, warm and orange.

One by one, they stepped back through. WHOOSH!

They landed back on the living room carpet, right where they'd started.

Milo's LEGO tower still stood tall. Juno's dinosaur toy sat where she'd dropped it. Theo's tablet glowed quietly on the rug.

But one thing was different. On the carpet sat one tiny, sparkly black rock. It was still faintly warm.

"Souvenir," said Blaze, winking from inside the brick. Then the glow faded to an ordinary gray.

Juno picked up the little rock and held it close. "From a real volcano."

Milo grinned. "Best brick ever."

Theo yawned a giant yawn. "Best field trip ever."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Sleep tight, little explorers.

fact_pack.summary: Volcanoes are places where melted rock, ash, and gas escape from deep inside the Earth. Some erupt gently and often, like Hawaii's Kilauea, while others, like Vesuvius or Krakatoa, produced huge explosions that changed history.

facts.text: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape from underground.
Molten rock is called magma underground, and lava once it flows out onto the surface.
Most volcanoes form along the edges of Earth's moving plates, where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.
The 'Ring of Fire' is a horseshoe belt around the Pacific Ocean holding about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes formed over a 'hotspot' of rising hot rock deep inside the Earth, not at the edge of a plate.
Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, erupting almost continuously for decades.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is Earth's largest active volcano by volume, rising over 4,000 meters above sea level.
Shield volcanoes are wide with gentle slopes, like Hawaii's; stratovolcanoes are tall, steep cones, like Mount Fuji.
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, burying the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under thick ash.
Roman writer Pliny the Younger watched the Vesuvius eruption and described it in letters, so scientists now call this explosive type a 'Plinian' eruption.
Krakatoa's 1883 eruption made a sound so loud it was heard about 3,000 miles away on Rodrigues Island.
Krakatoa's eruption caused giant tsunami waves that struck nearby coasts, making it one of the deadliest volcanic disasters in history.
In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced history's largest recorded eruption, and its ash helped make 1816 the 'Year Without a Summer' in Europe and America.
On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted right after the largest landslide ever recorded slid off its side.
The Mount St. Helens eruption blew about 1,300 feet off the mountain's summit while scientists were studying the volcano up close.
Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano whose last huge eruption happened about 640,000 years ago; scientists see no sign it will erupt soon.
In 1963, a new island named Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland as an underwater volcano kept erupting.
Iceland has many volcanoes because it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of Earth's plates pull apart.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, about 13.6 miles (22 km) high, nearly three times taller than Mount Everest.
Volcanologists use seismographs to detect tiny earthquakes and satellites to spot ground swelling, both early warning signs of an eruption.
Volcanic ash breaks down into very fertile soil, which is why many farmers live and grow crops near volcanoes despite the risk.
